This work identifies dual CA/ChE inhibition as a promising complementary strategy for AD and related disorders: CA inhibition mitigates Aβ-induced oxidative, inflammatory, and neurovascular stress, whilst ChE inhibition supports cholinergic neurotransmission and memory consolidation.

items.title: Discovery of sub-nanomolar and highly selective L-shaped carbonic anhydrase II inhibitors via amino-sugar-tail modification
Design, Synthesis, and Investigation of the Therapeutic Effects of Center-targeted Tyrosinase Inhibitors on Parkinson’s Disease
Urchin-Like Mesoporous Silica Nanoparticles Lower Intraocular Pressure through PARP1 Inhibition
items.abstract: Elevated intraocular pressure (IOP) drives glaucoma progression, yet durable control is limited by incomplete mechanistic targeting and inefficient anterior-segment drug delivery. Here, we identify poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase 1 (PARP1) hyperactivation as a redox-sensitive control node governing conventional outflow failure. In human trabecular meshwork and Schlemm’s canal tissues, upregulated PARP1, following oxidative stress, enforces nuclear retention of the ataxia telangiectasia mutated–NF-κB essential modulator (ATM–NEMO) complex. This suppresses cytoplasmic protein kinase B–endothelial nitric oxide synthase (AKT–eNOS) signaling and depletes intracellular nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+), effectively coupling DNA damage responses to nitric oxide deficiency and metabolic collapse. To reprogram this dual enzymatic–metabolic disturbance, we engineer a geometry-enhanced, pH-gated urchin-like mesoporous nanoplatform (hereafter denoted PUON@NMOF) that enables spatially segregated codelivery of the PARP1 inhibitor niraparib and the NAD+ precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide. The spiny nanoarchitecture enhances corneal adhesion and trans-epithelial transport, while the metal–organic framework (MOF) shell provides switchable release under mildly acidic microenvironments. Topical administration achieves preferential accumulation in outflow tissues, restores NAD+ pools, reactivates AKT–eNOS signaling and produces synergistic IOP reduction across distinct glaucoma models. These findings define the redox–PARP1 axis as a druggable vulnerability and establish materials-enabled dual-pathway correction as a strategy for precision modulation of outflow biomechanics.

items.title: Synergistic Lewis Base Organocatalysis and Electrocatalysis for the Enantioselective Construction of α‐Fluorinated Quaternary Stereocenters
items.abstract: The construction of α‐fluorinated quaternary stereocenters—a structural motif of high value in pharmaceuticals and bioactive molecules—remains a formidable synthetic challenge due to inherent steric and stereoelectronic constraints. Herein, we report a synergistic strategy combining chiral isothiourea (ITU) organocatalysis with electrochemistry, enabling the direct and highly enantioselective α‐alkylation of bench‐stable fluorinated acetic esters with both silyl enol ethers and allylsilanes. This approach integrates anodic single‐electron oxidation with asymmetric Lewis base catalysis, converting in situ‐generated disubstituted C1‐ammonium enolates into configurationally well‐defined, chiral ITU‐bound α‐carbonyl tertiary radical intermediates. Subsequent stereocontrolled radical cross‐coupling with SOMOphilic partners furnishes a broad range of esters bearing α‐fluorinated quaternary stereocenters in high yields (up to 95%) and excellent enantioselectivities (up to 99% ee). This work not only fills a significant gap in the single‐electron chemistry of disubstituted C1‐ammonium enolates but also provides a versatile platform for the rapid assembly of optically active α‐fluorinated quaternary carbonyl compounds, with significant potential in drug discovery and complex molecule synthesis.

items.title: Safranine T‐Derived Activable Photosensitizer to Synergistically Regulate the RSS/ROS Dynamic Equilibrium for Boosted Photosensitization
items.abstract: Photodynamic therapy (PDT) eliminates lesions like tumors via reactive oxygen species (ROS)‐mediated oxidative damage. However, tumors overexpress reactive sulfur species (RSS) that scavenge cytotoxic ROS, endowing cancer cells with strong antioxidant resistance and weakening PDT efficacy. We fabricated a biosafe, readily available activatable photosensitizer ST‐DNBS based on safranine T (ST). ST‐DNBS selectively consumes RSS overexpressed in tumors and recovers photochemically active ST to produce massive ROS. For example, 6 µM ST‑DNBS depletes substantial glutathione (GSH), leading to a marked reduction in the characteristic absorbance of TNB 2− (5‐thio‐2‐nitrobenzoate dianion) at 412 nm in the DTNB (Ellman's reagent) assay relative to the control; ROS produced after 24 s of irradiation causes a 6.2‐fold decrease in the UV absorbance of 1,3‐diphenylisobenzofuran (DPBF). Tumor‐activatable ST‐DNBS depletes intracellular RSS to collapse tumor antioxidant systems, blocking ROS clearance and boosting intracellular ROS buildup. This RSS/ROS redox balance remodeling greatly enhances photodynamic activity, achieving a 90% tumor inhibition rate. Our RSS‐scavenging, tumor‐activated photosensitizer offers a practical strategy to overcome tumor antioxidant barriers and improve PDT antitumor performance.

items.title: Late-Stage Skeletal Editing of the Arylacetic Acid Pharmacophore: A Photocatalytic Route to Oxetan-3-ol Bioisosteres
items.abstract: Oxetan-3-ols are valuable carboxylic acid bioisosteres, but their late-stage access is limited. A mild, transition-metal-free photocatalytic decarboxylative coupling directly converts arylacetic acids into oxetan-3-ols. The protocol avoids organometallic reagents and is extended to electron-deficient acids and strained ketones. Lipophilicity increases by up to 2.5 log units; the indomethacin analogue retains COX-2 inhibition (IC50 = 191 nM) while weakening COX-1 (280 nM), shifting the selectivity index from 0.20 to 1.47, and potentially reducing gastrointestinal toxicity.

items.title: A Cryptic Cytochrome P450 Radical Cyclase Catalyzes Naphthalene-Ring Closure in Rifamycin Biosynthesis
items.abstract: The enzymatic assembly of the 8-hydroxynaphthalene chromophore in rifamycins presents a classic biosynthetic paradox: the off-PKS precursor, prorifamycin A (1a), readily suffers nonenzymatic deoxygenative collapse in solution into the aberrant product 8-deoxynaphthoquinones. Here, using in cellulo genetic manipulation, stepwise pathway reconstitution, in vitro enzymatic assays, molecular docking, and DFT calculations, we identified Rif-Orf0 to be a cytochrome P450 radical cyclase. Rif-Orf0 converted 1a to the 8-hydroxy-7,8-dihydronaphthalenoid intermediate prorifamycin B (1b) through a low-barrier biradical cyclization, and the RifS/RifT dehydrogenase pair rapidly captured and oxidatively aromatized 1b to 34a-deoxyrifamycin W (2). This Rif-Orf0 and RifS/RifT enzymatic cascade outcompeted the spontaneous deoxygenative shunting that afforded 8-deoxynaphthalene-type rifamycins, thereby enforcing the production of 8-hydroxynaphthalenoid rifamycins. This study expanded the catalytic repertoire of cytochrome P450 enzymes and resolved a long-standing question in rifamycin biosynthesis by characterizing how tailoring enzymes canalized reactive intermediates from spontaneous reactions toward defined natural product architectures.

items.title: N-(Pyridin-2-yl)ureas incorporating an arylsulfonamide pharmacophore as potential adjuvants in lung cancer therapy
Synthesis, Characterization, and In Vitro Evaluation of Carbonate- and Carbamate-Based Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug Conjugates for Potential Central Nervous System Delivery
items.abstract: : Low brain bioavailability of non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) has, in part, limited the potential of these molecules as central nervous system (CNS) drugs. NSAIDs linked to blood-brain barrier (BBB) shuttles through carbonate and carbamate linkages, intended to deliver the parent drug to the brain via passive diffusion, were synthesized in 39-86% yields using a Steglich esterification. In vitro human plasma half-lives ranged from 2.0-6.4 hr, with a flurbiprofen-carbamate conjugate being most stable. Plasma-protein binding (PPB) was assessed and compared to the parent NSAIDs. Finally, passive BBB permeabilities, estimated via the parallel artificial membrane permeability assay for the BBB (PAMPA-BBB), and a variety of calculated physicochemical properties relevant to CNS drug delivery were determined. The NSAID conjugates presented herein have the potential to serve as one component of a multifaceted treatment strategy for CNS diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease (AD).

items.title: Discovery of Novel Triazole Derivatives with Potent and Selective Antifungal Activity against Candida glabrata
Structural Derivatization of Quinazolinone-Based PI3Kδ Inhibitor to Discover In Vivo Potent PI3Kδ/HDAC Bifunctional Therapeutic Agent against Solid Tumors
Tracking Carbon Oxidation States in Heterocycle-Forming Reactions
items.abstract: Despite the enormous variety of methods available for heterocycle construction, the corresponding reactions are most often organized according to functional groups, named transformations, or target ring systems rather than the oxidation states of carbon atoms present in the building blocks. In this perspective, we use the oxidation states of carbon as a unifying framework for heterocycle-forming reactions. Representative one- to five-atom building blocks are classified according to the number of atoms contributed towards the ring, the oxidation states of the carbon atoms involved in annulation reactivity, and their roles in bis-electrophilic, amphoteric, and bis-nucleophilic building blocks. By focusing on changes in carbon oxidation states, this framework relates seemingly disparate reactions, reveals connections between established synthetic methods, and identifies opportunities for the development of new chemistry. We anticipate that our work will offer both a useful pedagogical resource and a conceptual framework for advancing heterocycle synthesis.

items.title: Pharmacophore-Guided Discovery of Dual HER2/VEGFR2-Inhibitory 4-Anilinoquinazolines with In Vitro and In Vivo Antiproliferative and Antiangiogenic Activity
Novel Isatin-Thiazolidinone Hybrids as Dual Aldose Reductase and Sorbitol Dehydrogenase Inhibitors: Design, Synthesis, In Vitro and In Vivo Evaluation
Probing Different Chain Lengths and Saturation of the Fatty Acid Tail on Triglyceride-Mimetic Ionizable Lipids-Mediated siRNA Delivery
items.abstract: Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are regarded as a promising delivery vehicle for small interfering RNA (siRNA) for the treatment of acute liver failure. However, current LNPs show suboptimal lysosomal escape ability and biodegradability. Monoglycerides used as co-lipids show excellent lysosomal escape ability and biodegradability. However, they lack ionizable heads and only have a single hydrophobic tail. Accordingly, we design and synthesize five new triglyceride-mimetic ionizable lipids featuring variable fatty acid tail lengths and saturation levels, derived from triglyceride-like ionizable lipids that have two fatty acid tails and a tertiary amine. The ionizable lipids are susceptible to lipase-mediated degradation, thereby enhancing the biosafety of LNPs. Notably, among the synthetic lipids, 3-TG-OA displays distinct advantages in cellular internalization, lysosomal escape, biodistribution, and gene silencing efficacy. Our findings provide novel insights into the structure−activity relationship of fatty acid tails and establish a robust non-viral delivery platform for siRNA delivery.

items.title: Toward Consensus Definitions of Emerging Concepts in Medicinal Chemistry: A Community Call to Action
Bioorthogonal Engineering of Tumors with Bacterial Antigens Leverages Innate Immunity for Enhanced Adoptive T Cell Therapy
items.abstract: Substantial efforts in adoptive T-cell therapy have centered on boosting T-cell activity against tumors. However, a crucial yet overlooked factor is that the onset and maintenance of T-cell responses are highly dependent on innate immunity. Here, we developed a strategy of engineering tumors with bacterial antigens via click chemistry to cross-regulate innate-adaptive immunity, thereby enhancing the efficacy of adoptive T-cell therapy in solid tumors. The targeted delivery of bacterial antigens is mediated by azido sugar liposomes (TALP) for introducing azide groups on tumors and dibenzocyclooctyne-decorated bacterial membranes (DBCO-BM) to endow tumor cells with the innate immunogenicity of bacteria. Our study reveals that tumors with exposed bacterial antigens trigger innate immune responses for direct tumor killing and drive T-cell tumor infiltration to launch adaptive immunity. The antitumor functions of adoptive T cells are significantly augmented with the cross-activation of innate-adaptive immunity. This study highlights the potential of innate immunity in addressing the suboptimal response of adoptive T cells in solid tumors.

items.title: Multiscale Topological Transcriptomic Analysis for Alzheimer’s Disease Drug Repurposing
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a complex neurodegenerative disorder driven by multifactorial molecular mechanisms, which severely limit the efficacy of current therapeutic interventions. To accelerate the discovery of novel treatments, we propose a comprehensive computational framework integrating transcriptomic analysis, topological network characterization, machine learning (ML), and structure-based evaluation. By analyzing eight independent AD transcriptomic datasets, we constructed protein–protein interaction networks and implemented a multiscale topological differentiation strategy based on persistent homology and persistent spectral theory. This approach quantified the topological importance of each gene, prioritizing 67 nonredundant key genes. To bridge target identification with drug screening, we mapped these genes to the ChEMBL database, yielding 4,493 bioactivity records across five primary targets. We evaluated three ML algorithms across diverse molecular representations, including two natural language processing-derived molecular embeddings and a conventional molecular fingerprint. Deploying these predictive models for large-scale virtual screening of the DrugBank database yielded several promising repurposing candidates. Subsequent molecular docking against the target proteins GLP1R and CASP1 generated predicted binding poses for selected compounds. Physicochemical profiling identified differences relevant to their further assessment, although these computational results do not establish binding stability, pharmacokinetic suitability, or safety. This study not only identifies viable therapeutic candidates for AD but also provides a scalable, generalizable pipeline for target prioritization and drug discovery applicable to other complex human diseases.

items.title: 2-(3,5-difluoro-4-hydroxyphenyl)isoindoline-1,3-diones; a new family of immunomodulatory-type drugs diminish classical markers of cellular inflammation in LPS-challenged mouse macrophage cells
items.abstract: Herein, we report the synthesis, characterization, and preliminary biological evaluation of a family of new 2-(3,5-difluoro-4-hydroxyphenyl)isoindoline-1,3-diones. In total, a series of 21 compounds were produced using standard coupling procedures between substituted phthalate derivatives and appropriate anilines, with the desired materials being obtained in moderate to excellent yields. These materials demonstrated minimal cellular toxicity in RAW 264.7 cells, with all compounds maintaining >90% viability across each concentration tested, with most exceeding a 95% threshold even at the highest 30 μM dose. Screens against classical markers of cellular inflammation produced in LPS-activated RAW 264.7 cells revealed our materials to be broadly effective at reducing secreted levels of cellular nitrite, but less capable in attenuating TNF-α. Efficacy against IL-6 was notably more sporadic, with some compounds consistently elevating this cytokine, while others were substantially anti-inflammatory. In general, electronics seemed to play a role in associated activity, with donating substituents appearing to strengthen anti-inflammatory behavior more consistently than unsubstituted or electron-poor iterations, with certain isomeric variations providing the most consistently favorable immunomodulatory trends. Incorporation of the difluorophenol moiety suppressed cereblon binding action relative to classical IMiDs featuring a glutarimide ring. Ultimately, methyl-substituted compound 16 proved to be the most universally efficacious anti-inflammatory agent with notable attenuations observed for each marker examined, and at each concentration screened. However, amino-substituted materials 27, 18, and 31 were all individually superior at a single target of interest, specifically reducing secreted nitrite, TNF- α, or IL-6 to 36%, 69%, and 62% of control levels, respectively.

items.title: Development of systematically modified N-methylene-substituted saccharins as inhibitors and activity-based probes for serine proteases
items.abstract: Activity-based protein profiling has provided insight into the roles of many serine proteases in fundamental biological pathways, but currently available probes do not provide universal coverage of this family of enzymes. New probe structures with complementary reactivity could facilitate the study of poorly characterized serine proteases. N -methylene-substituted saccharins have been reported as covalent inhibitors for multiple serine proteases over the past several decades and could therefore serve as reactive groups in the design of activity-based probes. However, a systematic strategy for modifying the aromatic ring of saccharin has not been described. By accessing four regioisomeric late-stage halogen-containing intermediates, we synthesized a panel of compounds with alkyl, aryl, and alkynyl substitution at each available position of the saccharin aromatic ring as potential inhibitors and activity-based probes for serine proteases. Substrate assays and competitive activity-based protein profiling experiments reveal that the position and type of modification differentially impact the inhibition of several serine protease targets. Furthermore, we found that ethynyl-modified saccharin structures serve as activity-based probes for multiple serine proteases, including the bacterial rhomboid protease GlpG. Our studies demonstrate the value of systematically modifying multiple sites on a scaffold and establish the N -methylene-substituted saccharin core as a new reactive group for developing activity-based probes for serine proteases.

items.title: Design and Biological Evaluation of Cdc20 Inhibitors via Fragment Merging: A Computationally Proposed Adjacent Lateral Sub-Pocket Hypothesis
Aryl Palladium Acetates as Highly Active Species in Intermolecular Heck Reactions of Hindered Olefins
items.abstract: Despite decades of development since the early 1970s, the intermolecular Heck reaction of hindered tri- and tetrasubstituted olefins with aryl halides has remained a challenge. Traditional approaches relied on rate-acceleration by directing groups or high reactivity of cationic arylpalladium species generated from triflates and diazonium salts. Herein, we report the first general and efficient Heck coupling between trisubstituted alkenes (and selected tetrasubstituted olefins) with aryl iodides and bromides. Our protocol employs simple PdCl2 or Pd(OAc)2 as precatalyst and needs no directing groups. It features an exceptionally broad substrate scope, accommodating diverse (hetero)aryl halides and both acyclic and cyclic olefins, and the reaction proceeds efficiently on a gram scale with remarkably low palladium loadings. The practical value of this method is highlighted by its application in concise synthesis of several pharmaceutically relevant motifs. Mechanistically, HRMS and DFT calculations revealed that phosphine-free complexes of arylpalladium acetates─either monomer [(Ar)Pd(OAc)] or its paddlewheel dimer with bridging acetates─serve as the key active species. These species exhibit minimal steric hindrance, a high partial positive charge, and high electrophilicity at the palladium center, synergistically facilitating the binding and rapid insertion of hindered alkenes.

items.title: A Mitochondria-Targeted CPI-613 Derivative Overcomes Gemcitabine Resistance and Reduces Hepatic Metastasis in Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: Gemcitabine-resistant pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) can acquire an oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)-high phenotype, creating a therapeutically exploitable vulnerability. Here, we developed compound 17, a triphenylphosphonium-conjugated CPI-613 derivative that suppresses pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) activity and mitochondrial respiration. By perturbing oxidative metabolism and redox homeostasis, 17 induced mitochondrial dysfunction and ferroptotic cell death, with PANC-1-GemR cells displaying greater sensitivity than parental PANC-1 cells. This selectivity translated in vivo: 17 outperformed gemcitabine in resistant xenografts and dose-dependently suppressed syngeneic Panc02 tumors. Compound 17 also attenuated EMT-associated phenotypes and hepatic metastatic burden without overt toxicity. These findings identify OXPHOS dependence as an actionable vulnerability in drug-resistant PDAC and position 17 as a promising mitochondria-targeted candidate for treating PDAC and limiting hepatic metastasis.

items.title: Discovery of First-in-Class hCA II/ROCK Dual Inhibitors with Both IOP-Lowering and Retinal Neuroprotective Activities for the Treatment of Glaucoma
items.abstract: Glaucoma is the leading cause of irreversible blindness worldwide. Current first-line therapies frequently yield suboptimal intraocular pressure (IOP) control. Furthermore, many patients develop progressive visual field loss despite adequate pressure management. To address this gap, we developed a class of first-in-class dual-target inhibitors against carbonic anhydrase II (CA II) and Rho-associated coiled-coil-containing protein kinase (ROCK). Among them, A3 showed 6250-fold higher hCA II inhibitory potency than the initial fragment with favorable selectivity and 1.2-/1.7-fold higher ROCK1/2 inhibitory activity than fasudil. In vivo, A3 produced potent and sustained IOP reduction across multiple models. Notably, in the DBA/2J spontaneous glaucoma model, it potently lowered IOP and preserved retinal structural integrity. Meanwhile, A3 attenuated retinal ganglion cell apoptosis via its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, thereby conferring optic neuroprotection with favorable systemic safety. Overall, A3 overcomes key limitations of current antiglaucoma drugs and represents a promising candidate for combined IOP-lowering and optic neuroprotective therapy.

items.title: Nanozyme-Fortified Probiotics with Antioxidant and Anti-Infection Properties for Synergistic Living Therapeutics of Infected Diabetic Wounds
items.abstract: Living probiotics are receiving considerable attention in serving as biosafe and superb antibacterial agents for infected wound healing. However, the inadequate reactive oxygen species (ROS) scavenging capacity compromises the therapeutic effect of probiotics for infected diabetic wounds with high oxidative stress. Herein, we develop a nanozyme-fortified probiotic (NFP) orchestrating an excellent antioxidative activity and broad-spectrum antibacterial properties for synergistic living therapeutics of infected diabetic wounds. The Cu-doped zinc metal–organic framework (CDN) is synthesized to provide a bimetallic biomimetic Cu/Zn site and is uniformly anchored on the surface of Lacticaseibacillus rhamnosus GG (LGG). The resultant NFP exhibits four types of enzyme-like catalytic activities for ROS scavenging and demonstrates an excellent antioxidant capability. The superior intracellular antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects of NFP are also perceived, ascribed to the regulation of cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction, arachidonic acid metabolism, and signaling by interleukins in the cell. The secretion promotion of antimicrobial short-chain fatty acids is triggered by CDN regulation for the physiological activities of LGG, eliciting the well-balanced antibacterial activity of NFP. As demonstrated by the rat model of infected diabetic wounds, application of NFP significantly eradicates bacterial infection, alleviates inflammation by ROS elimination, and directs polarization to M2 macrophages, thereby accelerating wound closure. This work provides a promising living material-based tactic consisting of microbial therapy and catalytic nanomaterials for treating infected diabetic wounds.

items.title: MolCodon: A Codon-Based Molecular Language for Interpretable Structural Representation and Similarity Search
items.abstract: Molecular representation determines which aspects of chemical structure can be learned, compared, and interpreted in computational drug discovery. Existing encodings typically emphasize either compact string description, as in SMILES and SELFIES, or efficient similarity search, as in circular fingerprints. Although canonical SMILES already provides a deterministic string, its tokens are variable in width and carry no fixed chemical role. No existing representation simultaneously offers fixed-width, role-assigned tokenization, graph-level interpretability, pharmacophore annotation, and high-fidelity molecular reconstruction. Here, we introduce MolCodon, a codon-based molecular language that represents small molecules as deterministic sequences of fixed-width three-character tokens over a five-symbol alphabet, C, N, O, S, and X. Inspired by the triplet organization of the genetic code, MolCodon assigns chemically defined codon families to atoms, bonds, ring and branch topology, fused-ring references, pharmacophore features, bond mobility, charge, and stereochemistry. A deterministic graph traversal with ring-contiguity preservation produces sequences in which chemically meaningful substructures remain locally organized and traceable to the underlying molecular graph. Across approximately 2.9 million molecules from six commercial screening libraries, MolCodon achieved 98.93% InChIKey-level round-trip fidelity, supporting its use as a high-fidelity sequence representation for drug-like compounds. Across ten QSAR tasks, MolCodon-derived sparse sequence and trace features showed statistically supported advantages over the SMILES and SELFIES-based representations in most data sets while achieving competitive performance with classical fingerprints. These findings are supported by five repeated cross-validation and Tukey-adjusted pairwise comparisons. As an application of the representation, the MolCodon similarity engine decomposes molecular similarity into ring topology, branch context, attachment architecture, and pharmacophore correspondence, enabling interpretable scaffold-hopping searches. In a PARP1 virtual screening case study, MolCodon retrieved scaffold-diverse candidates using a known PARP-1 inhibitor Olaparib as the template compound. Together, these results establish MolCodon as a new molecular representation paradigm that transforms chemical graphs into high-fidelity, interpretable, and alignment-compatible codon sequences, opening a direct path for bioinformatics-inspired analysis of small-molecule chemical space. The MolCodon encoder, decoder, and similarity engine are freely available as open-source software at https://github.com/DurdagiLab/MolCodon.

items.title: Molecular Assembly Enumeration vs. 1D Dictionary Compression Across the Nano-DrugBank Small-Molecule Repository
items.abstract: Assembly Theory (AT) defines the Molecular Assembly Index (MA) as the minimal number of recursive bonddisjoint subgraph-joining steps required to construct a 2D molecular graph [1, 2, 4], whereas critics from Algorithmic Information Theory (AIT) contend that empirical MA rankings collapse to standard 1D dictionary compression applied to molecular strings [5, 6, 15]. Here, we evaluate MA against wrapped zlib (RFC 1950), headerless raw DEFLATE (RFC 1951), and header-free 256-ASCII Welch LZW across the Chodera Lab Nano-DrugBank small-molecule repository (N = 5,653, curated from DrugBank 4.5.0) [20–24] using the C++ branchand-bound solver (assemblycpp-v5) [4] under operating-system process isolation on an Apple M3 Ultra workstation. Applying RDKit valence sanitization, parent-fragment desalting (60 salts), stereochemistry-stripped Kekulé MDL V2000 serialization, and a 600 s per-subprocess wall-clock timeout yielded 5,520 resolved records (97.65%; MA in [1, 36], median MA = 14, median subprocess wall time 15.42 ms, mean 3,051 ms; conditional on the inspected two-argument repository runner pending a hash-logged rerun), 35 RDKit valence rejections (0.62%), and 98 computationally unresolved valid graphs (1.73%): 87 with subprocess runtime right-censored at 600 s (median Nheavy = 77) and 11 macrocycles/polypeptides (median Nheavy = 128) explicitly logging the solver's internal Subgraph enumeration limit reached (ENUM_MAX = 50,000,000) diagnostic between 375.8 and 578.2 s. Among resolved records (median Nheavy = 23), 2,429 (44.00%) satisfy MA ≥ 15 [1, 2]. Per-character compression ratios span more than twofold ranges within fixed-MA slices, and in in-sample linear ordinary least-squares (OLS) models adjusting for heavy-atom count (Nheavy), compressed lengths explain 38.6% (DEFLATE: partial r = +0.6212) and 32.0% (Welch LZW: partial r = +0.5656) of Nheavy-adjusted MA variance on stereochemistrystripped canonical parent SMILES (38.4% and 31.7% across n = 5,274 unique parent strings; 42.9% and 38.8% on Kekulé charge/isotope-stripped V2000 graph SMILES, or 42.3% and 38.1% across n = 5,254 unique keys). Across all tested specifications, 57.1%–68.3% of in-sample Nheavy-adjusted linear MA variance remains unexplained, showing that the evaluated 1D SMILES compressors and 2D MA are positively correlated yet not linearly interchangeable.

items.title: Selectivity for Fe versus Carbonyl Centered Silylation in Low-Valent β-Diketiminate Fe Complexes
items.abstract: Understanding the changes in reactivity and selectivity engendered by weak-field supporting ligands and multimetallic complexes offers new opportunities in organometallic chemistry. Here, we examine the selectivity of reactions of silyl electrophiles with monometallic iron-carbonyl complexes, which can lead to silylation either at the metal to form a silyl complex, or at a CO ligand to give a carbyne complex. The first mode of reactivity is common with classic organometallic complexes, and the latter has been observed more recently with complexes with strong-field ligands. More recently, bridging CO complexes with weak-field β-diketiminate ligands have been observed to give carbyne products as well, implying that the bridging CO ligands are nucleophilic in this environment. However, it was not clear whether the key determinant of CO reactivity was the ligand field strength or the bridging of the CO ligand. Here, these influences are decoupled by studying silylation of monomeric iron(0) dicarbonyl and tricarbonyl complexes with the same weak-field β-diketiminate ligand. We show that silylation at the iron, at the CO, or at THF can dominate. A particularly interesting product comes from THF silylation, followed by nucleophilic attack by Fe to give ring-opening and very rapid migration of a transient iron-alkyl complex to CO. DFT studies confirm that the β-diketiminate supported complexes undergo much more rapid alkyl migration than the analogous reaction in classic cyclopentadienyliron complexes. Overall, this work gives insights into ligand effects on reactivity for silylation and on alkyl insertion/CO migration.

items.title: Temporal programming of pH in enzyme-encapsulated artificial cells: role of differential membrane permeability
items.abstract: Coupling autocatalytic reaction networks and membrane-regulated transport of species within confined compartments provides a powerful strategy for engineering programmable dynamics in artificial cells. Here, we demonstrate temporal control of pH in phospholipid vesicles by encapsulating glucose oxidase (GOx) and urease enzymes, which respectively generate acidic and basic products from glucose and urea. We first explore the glucose-GOx reaction under confinement within the synthetic vesicles, combining experiments with simulations to find conditions for a pH clock reaction; a switch from base to acid after a time delay. We show that product entrapment results in a pH gradient between the internal and external solution and accelerates the reaction. By varying lipid composition, we find that the clock time increases with membrane thickness, consistent with glucose permeability regulating reaction kinetics under confinement. Building on these transport-limited dynamics, we couple the antagonistic GOx and urease reactions either in separate vesicle populations or within the same vesicle. Co-encapsulation produces an autonomous pH pulse in base, driven by differential membrane transport and product localisation. The pH clock and pulse amplitude and timescales can be tuned by initial concentrations, oxygen transfer rate from the air and volume fraction of the vesicles. Together, these findings establish how membrane-regulated feedback, substrate delay and product retention can be used to control the timescales of pH changes in artificial cells.

items.title: Visible-Light-Induced Three-Component Minisci-Type Trifluoroalkylation of Electron-Deficient Heteroaromatics
items.abstract: The combination of electron-poor heterocycles and trifluoromethyl motifs is widely found in pharmaceuticals, making the development of methods for the simultaneous introduction of these two features highly desirable. Herein, we report a fast, acid-free, metal-free, photocatalyst-free, and operationally simple multicomponent approach for the trifluoroalkylation of electron-poor heterocycles under aerobic conditions. The method relies on the ability of trifluoromethyl thianthrenium triflate to generate CF3 radicals and proceeds through a polarity-reversal cascade strategy, employing electron-rich alkenes as linkers. A broad range of alkenes and heterocycles were evaluated, and the chemo- and regioselectivities of the process were thoroughly investigated. Furthermore, mechanistic studies revealed that multiple pathways contribute to the formation of the desired products.

items.title: Functionalized liposomes in cancer immunotherapy: Engineering strategies and therapeutic opportunities
Isosteres in Chemistry
items.abstract: Dating back to 1919 with its coinage by Irving Langmuir, isosterism has continuously evolved over the past century. While ever changing, the overall idea has remained constant; isosteres are interchangeable groups or atoms which modulate a compound’s chemical properties. At a fundamental level, understanding the key concepts of isosterism has allowed for the development of a framework which enables intellectual compound design. As the undercurrent of all chemical innovation is the drive to discover, synthesize, or improve compounds such that their implementation improves their desired uses, isosteric rationale has been adopted by all areas of chemistry. However, the extent of intentional isosteric reasoning varies drastically across fields. While booming to popularity within the medicinal chemistry field with the creation of the bioisostere subcategory of isosterism, other fields like physical, inorganic, materials, and agricultural chemistry rarely attribute compound design changes to isosterism. In this review, we will cover the conceptualization and evolution of the term isosterism, provide an update on current medicinal chemistry application of isosteres, and highlight both intentional and unrecognized implementation of isosterism outside of the medicinal field. In both medicinal and non-medicinal chemistry applications, the effect of isosteric replacements will be emphasized. This collation of the wide range of isosteric replacements elucidates the breadth of applicability of the isostere concept with an aim of demonstrating how this inherently broad concept offers the potential to improve compound design across all areas of chemistry.

items.title: GENESIS: Potency-Graded Contrastive Learning for Generative Molecular Design and Drug Repurposing in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma
items.abstract: Computational drug discovery typically binarizes bioactivity, discarding the graded doseresponse signal needed for lead prioritization. We introduce Potency-Graded Contrastive Learning (PGCL), projecting frozen molecular language-model embeddings into a 128dimensional space via an ordinal contrastive objective, six-tier negative taxonomy, and tier-margin ranking. Across three seeds, PGCL achieves Spearman ρ = 0.555 ± 0.003 for potency ordering and target-switch AUROC = 0.967, outperforming flat-contrastive and binaryclassification ablations and roughly doubling ECFP4 activity-cliff discrimination. Among six generative architectures, our reinforcement-learning method CRAVE (Contrastive Reward-Aligned VAE Exploration) significantly exceeds non-RL baselines on OSCC potency after Bonferroni correction (p = 0.016). The frozen model transfers to lung adenocarcinoma without retraining — strongly along the PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis (PIK3CA ρ=0.688, MTOR ρ=0.614, AKT1 ρ=0.583, EGFR ρ=0.561) but only modestly when pooled across all 16 LUAD-relevant targets (ρ=0.207, n=52,373). An integrated docking, ADMET, network-pharmacology, and leadoptimization pipeline screens 23,308 repurposing candidates, prioritizing 46 Tier-1 candidates, including 13 triple-validated elite compounds, with transparently reported safety pass rates (14.6%) traced to an EGFR/aniline training-corpus skew. The pipeline runs end-to-end on consumer-grade hardware, with code and protocols enabling transfer to other cancers.

items.title: Site-Controlled Reaction Routing for Electrocatalytic Small Molecule Transformations
items.abstract: The electrocatalytic conversion of small molecules, including CO2, nitrate, and their C–N coupling, offers a sustainable route to fuels, fertilizers, and high-value chemicals, potentially replacing energy-intensive thermochemical processes. Yet, the field remains challenged by poor selectivity and sluggish kinetics. The fundamental bottleneck is not a lack of active materials but our inability to control the complex behavior of reaction intermediates such as *COOH, *NO, *CO, and *NHO, which compete for active sites and diverge into parallel pathways during multistep proton-coupled electron transfer. Traditional catalyst design, guided by the d-band center model and Sabatier principle, optimizes a single adsorption energy descriptor. This approach reaches an inherent ceiling when intermediates demand conflicting binding affinities, for example, when strong adsorption of one species inhibits desorption of another. Moreover, it overlooks structural factors of intermediates like adsorption orientation and coupling geometry as well as noncovalent influences from proton supply, local pH, and interfacial water structure, which critically shape the reaction pathway under operating conditions. Over the past several years, our group has developed a site-controlled “reaction routing” strategy that moves beyond passive optimization toward active intervention in intermediate behavior. In this account, we achieve this through rational design of active sites and their local environment, organized into three hierarchical levels. At the first level, single site intrinsic regulation modulates the electronic structure of metal centers via static coordination units or dynamic ligand protonation, precisely balancing adsorption strengths and enabling high selectivity across a broad potential window. At the second level, multisite cooperative regulation uses heterometallic dual centers or proton donor sites to steer intermediate coupling modes and adsorption orientations, bypassing scaling relations. At the third level, interfacial microenvironment remodeling leverages active sites to induce water molecule rearrangement, reconstruct hydrogen bond networks to accelerate proton transfer, or constrain gas coverage to modulate adsorbed species. These effects direct the reaction from the dual perspectives of macroscopic mass transport and interfacial thermodynamics, suppressing competing pathways while favoring desired product channels. These three levels, from the inner to the outer and from electronic to interfacial, together constitute a complete framework for site-controlled reaction routing. We further discuss remaining challenges, including dynamic adaptability under fluctuating potentials, synergy rules among regulatory dimensions, the integration of machine learning for accelerated catalyst design, and the transition from model systems to practical electrolyzer devices. This account offers new design principles and a roadmap for advancing sustainable chemical synthesis through rational intermediate management, where each reaction step is deliberately steered toward the intended product.

items.title: SeqA-mediated sister loci cohesion regulates the efficiency and fidelity of DNA double-strand break repair across the E. coli genome
items.abstract: In Escherichia coli , SeqA-mediated cohesion at snap loci on the right replichore persists longer, but its role in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair remains untested. Here, we show that site-specific DSBs at snap loci confer higher cell survival than nonsnap loci. With perturbations affecting sister cohesion [Δ seqA , topoisomerase IV overexpression (T4-OE)], this survival advantage was progressively reduced, with the combined Δ seqA T4-OE strain retaining only a transient advantage. The increased survival correlates with faster repair, reflected by rapid restoration of locus copy number and shorter-lived, thinner RecA–green fluorescent protein filaments. Consistent with more accurate repair, snap loci exhibited lower mutation accumulation under normal and antibiotic stress conditions. Comparative genome analysis of E. coli strains revealed higher GATC motif counts and higher sequence conservation. Together, these findings suggest that the chromosomal organization associated with prolonged sister cohesion at snap loci promotes efficient homologous recombination–mediated DSB repair and contributes to genome conservation.

items.title: Immune infiltrate predicts response to αPD1/αCTLA4 but not αPD1 and distinguishes programs of primary resistance in metastatic melanoma
items.abstract: While immune-checkpoint blockade (ICB) has revolutionized treatment of metastatic melanoma, the identification of robust biomarkers to predict the relative efficacy of single versus combination ICB has been challenging. We performed a meta-analysis of eight cohorts of patients treated with anti–PD-1 ( n = 290), anti–CTLA-4 ( n = 175), and combination anti–PD-1/anti–CTLA-4 ( n = 51) with pretreatment tumor sequencing and clinical annotations. Surprisingly, the increased response rate to combination anti–PD-1/anti–CTLA-4 compared to anti–PD-1 monotherapy was observed only in highly immune infiltrated tumors, and not in immune-low tumors. Stratifying tumors by high or low frequency of immune cells also distinguished context-dependent programs of primary resistance to single and combination ICB. Notably, hypoxia-related pathways were enriched in nonresponders to anti–PD-1 ICB in immune-high, but not immune-low, tumors. Using an independent cohort of patients with scRNA-seq data, we observed that correlates of hypoxia were associated with increased stromal tumor receptor-ligand interactions. As proof of concept, selective inhibition of HIF-2α, a component of the hypoxia pathway and highly expressed in endothelial cells and fibroblasts, in combination with anti–PD-1, controlled tumor growth in mouse models of highly immune-infiltrated tumors but not poorly immune-infiltrated tumors. Our work demonstrates how stratification by tumor immune characteristics and clinical features can lead to the rational discovery of novel therapeutic targets.

items.title: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) binds talin and is anchored at the postsynaptic density by direct PDZ interactions
items.abstract: Cyclin-dependent kinase-like 5 (CDKL5) is a serine/threonine kinase essential for brain development and function. Mutations in CDKL5 cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a severe early-onset epileptic encephalopathy associated with impaired synapse formation and function. However, how CDKL5 mutations disrupt synaptic function remains unclear. Here, we show that the major neuronal isoform of CDKL5 contains a C-terminal PDZ domain–binding motif that mediates direct binding to PSD-95 and SHANK PDZ domains and recruits CDKL5 to the postsynaptic density. Disrupting this motif mislocalized CDKL5, reduced dendritic spine density, and impaired spine maturation. We also show that the CDKL5 kinase domain binds the R8 rod domain of the mechanosensitive scaffold talin. Mutation of the talin-binding interface or reduced cellular contractility altered CDKL5 positioning relative to focal adhesions. These findings define how CDKL5 is targeted to synapses, suggest that talin mechanoswitching may position CDKL5 kinase activity, and highlight the importance of C-terminal anchoring for interpreting pathogenic truncations.

items.title: Clearance of erythrocytes after subarachnoid hemorrhage: Cranial lymphatic and dural pathways
items.abstract: The clearance of toxic blood products from the brain after subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is critical for neurological recovery, yet the precise anatomical pathways and cellular mechanisms responsible for this process remain poorly defined. Using murine models of both arterial perforation and low-rate intracisternal injection, we have mapped a comprehensive, multifaceted network of red blood cell (RBC) distribution and clearance. We found that, while RBCs accessed peripheral lymphatic vessels via cranial nerves, an extensive distribution of extravasated erythrocytes could also be observed sequestered within nonendothelial, collagen-lined interstitial channels flanking the major dural venous sinuses. By day 2 post-SAH, regional macrophages actively cleared some trapped erythrocytes. These findings provide a detailed spatiotemporal framework of SAH blood clearance, revealing promising anatomical and cellular targets to accelerate stroke recovery.

items.title: SMAD4 loss drives cancer chromosomal instability through transcription-replication conflict–associated replication stress
items.abstract: Cancer chromosomal instability (CIN) drives tumor evolution through generating structural and numerical chromosome aberrations. However, its molecular determinants remain poorly characterized. Here, we uncover a yet unrecognized role for the tumor suppressor SMAD4 as a key regulator of chromosomal stability. Mechanistically, loss of SMAD4 causes replication stress by promoting transcription-replication conflicts (TRCs) and induces subsequent mitotic errors, leading to the concomitant emergence of structural and numerical CIN. While the tumor suppressor function of SMAD4 has been predominantly attributed to transforming growth factor–β signaling, we find that its role in genome maintenance operates via bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) signaling and its transcriptional target gene ID3 . Consequently, inhibition of BMP signaling mimics the loss of SMAD4 , while reexpression of SMAD4 or ID3 in SMAD4 -deficient colorectal or pancreatic cancer cells suppresses TRCs, replication stress, and mitotic errors. Our findings reveal a TRC- and replication stress–driven mechanism by which loss of BMP-SMAD4 signaling causes cancer CIN.

items.title: Targeting METTL3 protects against acetaminophen-induced liver injury through HAPTOGLOBIN/CD163 macrophage axis
items.abstract: Acetaminophen (APAP) overdose is the most common cause of drug-induced liver injury (DILI), with limited treatment options. N 6 -methyladenosine (m 6 A) is the most abundant internal epitranscriptomic modification in eukaryotic RNAs and is involved in various physiological and pathological processes, serving as a potential therapeutic target for many diseases. However, little is known about the role of m 6 A in DILI. Here, we found that intrahepatic expression of Methyltransferase-like 3 (METTL3), the core catalytic subunit of RNA m 6 A methyltransferase complex, was elevated in patients with DILI and mouse DILI models. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of METTL3, achieved via either Alb-Cre ERT2 –driven recombination or adeno-associated virus (AAV)–mediated delivery of Cre, significantly protected from APAP-induced hepatotoxicity in both male and female mice. Mechanistically, hepatic METTL3 deficiency reduced m 6 A deposition on acute-phase protein haptoglobin ( Hp ) transcripts and promoted Hp transcription and translation in hepatocytes. Increased HP secreted by hepatocytes bound to its receptor CD163, expressed explicitly on macrophages, and induced highly phagocytic and anti-inflammatory polarization of macrophages, finally reducing APAP-induced hepatic injury. Moreover, two different METTL3 inhibitors, JNJ64619178 and STM2457, effectively alleviated APAP-induced liver injury. Our study thus demonstrated that hepatic inhibition of METTL3 protected against APAP-induced liver injury by promoting the cross-talk between hepatocytes and macrophages through HP/CD163, underscoring the potential of targeting METTL3 as a promising therapy for APAP overdose.

items.title: Disulfiram inhibits pyroptosis and apoptosis through multiple complementary mechanisms
items.abstract: Gasdermins (GSDMs) execute pyroptosis by forming lytic pores in the plasma membrane that release IL-1 cytokines and promote cell swelling and membrane rupture. Their key roles in infection, inflammation and cancer make GSDMs attractive therapeutic targets. Here we systematically investigate how disulfiram, an approved drug for treating alcoholism, inhibits pyroptosis and identify multiple complementary mechanisms. First, disulfiram inhibits processing of procaspase-1 to caspase-1. Second, disulfiram inhibits caspases from processing human GSDMD to release the lytic N-terminal domain (GSDMD Nterm ). Third, disulfiram structurally modifies GSDMD Nterm . Fourth, disulfiram partitions into membranes, where it remains embedded, changes membrane properties and prevents GSDMD Nterm insertion. Similarly, disulfiram blocks intrinsic apoptosis by inhibiting procaspase-3 activation, caspase-3 cleavage of human GSDME, and GSDME Nterm pore formation. Furthermore, we show that two other GSDMD inhibitors, necrosulfonamide and dimethyl fumarate also inhibit GSDM-induced cell death through multiple complementary mechanisms. These multilevel inhibitory mechanisms deepen our understanding of strategies to target GSDM-mediated cell death pathways.

items.title: Brominated polyunsaturated lipids from the marine sponge Xestospongia sp.: dual TDP1/TDP2 inhibitory activity and cardioprotective potential
Rationally Designed Paracetamol-Conjugated Porphyrinoids Potentiate NIR Photodynamic Therapy, Systemic Antitumor Immunity, and Abscopal Effect
A generative neural network architecture for structure elucidation
items.abstract: Determining molecular structure is central to chemistry. One-dimensional (1D) 1H and 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy is a standard technique in small molecule structure determination, but deducing a structure from these spectra remains challenging because of the vast chemical space involved. Deep learning models that predict structures directly from NMR data have shown potential in navigating this space, but are trained largely on simulated spectra and perform poorly on real experimental data. Here we present a transformer model trained purely on experimental NMR data from approximately 1 million molecules, which takes 1D 1 H and 13 C NMR peak lists together with molecular weight (readily obtained from mass spectrometry) and generates candidate structures as SMILES strings. On a held-out test set, our model identified the correct structure among 15 candidates for 56.6% of molecules with up to 19 heavy atoms (34.8% overall). On a benchmark of 86 experimental spectra, it was more than four times as accurate as the published NMR2Struct model at every candidate pool size, while generating more chemically valid candidates. Even when the exact structure was missed, its best candidates remained structurally close to the target, and its incorrect candidates retained many of the target’s functional groups, making them useful starting points for structure elucidation. These results demonstrate that training on experimental spectra substantially improves structure prediction from routine 1D NMR data.

items.title: Diastereoselective synthesis of 3-monosubstituted phthalides through the MCR of phthalaldehydic acid, sulfoxonium ylides and thiols
items.abstract: A Brønsted acid-catalyzed multicomponent reaction (MCR) of phthalaldehydic acids, stabilized sulfoxonium ylides, and thiols is developed for the synthesis of 3-monosubstituted phthalides, a structural motif of considerable relevance to natural product and medicinal chemistry. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions and a ords the desired phthalide products featuring a thiol-functionalized side-chain in moderate to good yields with excellent anti-diastereoselectivity. The substrate scope encompasses di erent aliphatic thiols, sulfoxonium ylides, and substituted phthalaldehydic acids, although product stability during chromatographic purification limits isolated yields in some cases. In situ NMR monitoring reveals a two-step reaction pathway involving the rapid formation of a disubstituted sulfoxonium ylide intermediate, followed by slower product formation through a delayed catalytic cycle. The isolated intermediate also exhibits distinct reactivity toward other nucleophiles, enabling the synthesis of indole- and triazole-containing derivatives. Although enantioselective variants remain unsuccessful, the developed methodology provides an approach to structurally diverse phthalides of interest in natural product chemistry and o ers further insight into the mechanistic features of sulfoxonium ylide-based multicomponent reactions under Brønsted acid catalysis.

items.title: HFn-E2: a computationally designed human H-ferritin nanocage codelivering iron and the covalent GPX4 inhibitor ML210 for ferroptosis induction in lung cancer — design, PBPK scenario modelling, structure validation and human-data premise analysis
items.abstract: Ferroptosis induction by covalent inhibition of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) is a validated anticancer mechanism, but the most potent chemotype — the masked nitrile-oxide inhibitor ML210 — has never been formulated in a protein nanocage, and single-agent iron delivery is insufficient on its own. We present HFn-E2, a computationally designed human H-ferritin (HFn) cage intended to codeliver a mineralised iron core (target 1,000–2,000 Fe/cage) and ML210 (20–50/cage; Fe:ML210 ≈ 20:1–100:1) to transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1)-positive lung tumours, releasing both payloads upon lysosomal cage disassembly. The design combines a thermoresponsive-channel mutation (D44A) for thermal loading, a tHFn(+)-type endosomal-pH disassembly module (E61K/E64R with C-terminal truncationΔ160–182), and an optional MMP-cleavable shield reserved for a second version. A compartment PBPK scenario model, parameterised only from predecessor-formulation fits and literature anchors, predicts full-interval tumour coverage by free ML210 under all lysosomal-release scenarios, while the tumour:liver exposure ratio R reaches 0.60 in the realistic-best case and would require a ×8.34 tumour-uptake gain to reach 1.0 under honest liver accounting; MonteCarlo propagation (n = 1,000) gives R median 0.19–0.25 with P(R ≥ 1) ≤ 0.01, but coverage in 95.9% of draws. ESMFold structure validation anchored against two experimental structures (RMSD 0.62–0.71 Å) shows the engineered monomer within 0.36 Å of wild type, with no engineered site on the TfR1 contact surface. Human-data analyses (TCGA, DepMap 24Q4, UniProt) support the GPX4 dependency and MMP-9 premises, show GPX4 near-common-essentiality in lung lines (median Chronos−0.707,n=126), and — reported as found — do not support universal TFRC mRNA overexpression in lung adenocarcinoma. We also document a sequence discrepancy in the deposited tHFn(+) construct (PDB 9KAY carries E140K/E147K beyond the review-relayed definition). HFn-E2 is a fully computational design study with no experimental data; five pre-registered pilot experiments with frozen decision gates are defined to test it.

items.title: Supramolecular Regulation of the Enzymatic Dephosphorylation of Twin Phosphotyrosine Peptides
items.abstract: We report the design, preparation, and study of a supramolecular pseudopeptidic cage that selectively binds twin phosphotyrosine (pTyr–pTyr) peptides and modulates their enzymatic dephosphorylation in water. The receptor combines an expanded aromatic cavity specifically designed to encapsulate a twin Tyr-Tyr motif with peripheral Lys-derived ammonium groups that engage phosphate residues through electrostatic interactions. In addition to studying the cage’s binding properties through different experimental and computational techniques, we investigated the ability of the receptor to modulate the kinetics of the irreversible phosphate hydrolysis catalyzed by alkaline phosphatase (ALP). When different substrates are connected through irreversible catalytic reactions, forming a nascent network, the presence of a supramolecular protecting host, able to selectively bind these substrates, modifies the system outcome in a way that cannot be predicted from the mere comparison of individual binding constants. This leads to unexpected, emerging behaviors, altering the relative intermediate concentrations through time and therefore regulating the network response. We demonstrate the biochemical potential of this cage by protecting the twin pTyr–pTyr motif within the activation loop of JAK2 kinase from dephosphorylation by λ-protein phosphatase. Altogether, our results establish supramolecular substrate protection as an effective strategy to regulate multistep enzymatic reaction networks.

items.title: Nanogel structure shapes host-cell interactions and antibiotic performance against biofilm-associated and intracellular Staphylococcus aureus
items.abstract: Antibiotic treatment is often compromised by bacterial persistence within biofilms and host cells, contributing to recurrent infections and antimicrobial resistance.Here, a structurally diverse series of N-isopropylacrylamide (NIPAM)-based nanogels (NGs) is evaluated to deliver ceftiofur (CF) against Staphylococcus aureus , using bovine mastitis as a clinically relevant context. Surface chemistry and network architecture are varied to determine how NG structure influences biological interactions and antibiotic performance. Although NIPAM-based NGs are not bactericidal, their composition modulates bacterial surface hydrophobicity and biofilm formation, as well as macrophage inflammatory responses and cellular uptake. CF-NG formulations exhibit strong activity against established biofilms and intracellular S. aureus, with all formulations reducing intracellular bacterial burdens by at least two log units. Cationic NGs enable CF to reduce viable intracellular bacteria to undetectable levels despite the lower cellular uptake observed for cationic NGs without CF. Anionic NGs provide the most balanced profile, combining favorable cytocompatibility, broad immunomodulatory effects, high uptake, and strong antibiofilm and intracellular activity. Overall, the results establish NG structure as a key determinant of interactions with bacteria and host cells and of CF-NG efficacy, providing design principles for nanocarriers targeting biofilm-associated and intracellular S. aureus.

items.title: Genome Mining of Scorpion-Derived Streptomyces glaucescens SduA113: Discovery and Biosynthetic Pathway of Spilactamycins
items.abstract: Genome mining of Streptomyces glaucescens SduA113, derived from Buthus martensii Karsch, revealed a novel PKS-NRPS gene cluster (spi) sharing little homologous BGCs in public databases. A total of eight spilactamycins (1–8) correlated to this cluster were isolated using medium optimization and heterologous expression, with 4 exhibiting weak antibacterial activity and strong anti-inflammatory activity. Furthermore, bioinformatic analysis and gene inactivation experiments enabled us to propose a complete biosynthetic pathway for spilactamycins.

items.title: ICPoly: An Automated Molecular Dynamics Workflow for Characterizing Structure, Dynamics, and Transport in Polymer Ion-Exchange Membranes
items.abstract: Predicting ionic transport in polymer ion-exchange membranes requires molecular models that connect polymer structure and hydration with local dynamics and collective charge transport. Here, we present ICPoly, an automated molecular dynamics workflow for characterizing the structure, dynamics, and ionic conductivity of these membranes. ICPoly integrates sequence-controlled polymer construction and fragment-based GAFF2 parameterization with staged classical and machine-learned equilibration, molecular-connectivity monitoring, and color-field nonequilibrium molecular dynamics (NEMD). Constant-field and constant-current formulations are implemented through modified Nosé–Hoover integrators in the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE), while trajectory analysis characterizes the membrane structure and sulfonic acid deprotonation and predicts quasielastic neutron scattering (QENS) spectra. The workflow is demonstrated for hydrated Nafion 212 in its proton and sodium forms using the reactive machine-learned UMA-s-1p2 potential. For representative Nafion-like fragments, UMA-s-1p2 achieves energy and force root-mean-square errors of 2.17 meV/atom and 41.84 meV/Å relative to density functional theory. The simulations reproduce the hydration-dependent decrease in density and reveal hydration-dependent changes in pore geometry and local organization, as well as incomplete sulfonic acid deprotonation. The two NEMD formulations yield similar velocity-based conductivity estimates. A displacement-based constant-field estimator shows faster apparent convergence but yields a substantially lower conductivity; it is adopted for subsequent calculations. Predicted proton and sodium conductivities increase with hydration, although proton conductivity is systematically underestimated and sodium conductivity is overestimated at low hydration. Overall, ICPoly provides a versatile and extensible computational framework that bridges polymer chemistry, molecular structure, dynamics, and ionic transport, enabling systematic investigations of structure–property relationships and facilitating the rational design of high-performance polymer materials.

items.title: Effect of Cu(II) Complexation on the Anticancer Activity of Zidovudine in the NCI-60 Human Tumor Cell Line Screen
items.abstract: Zidovudine (AZT, azidothymidine) was originally synthesized as a potential anticancer agent. Originally synthesized in 1964 by Jerome Horwitz at the Michigan Cancer Foundation during efforts to develop antitumor nucleoside analogues, AZT demonstrated insufficient anticancer activity in early evaluations and was not pursued further at that time. Despite its clinical success as an antiviral agent, AZT has continued to attract interest in its anticancer properties, including inhibition of telomerase activity, induction of DNA damage, modulation of cell-cycle progression, and disruption of survival signaling pathways. In the present study, AZT (NSC D-858683) and a Cu(II)-AZT complex (NSC D-858684) were evaluated by the National Cancer Institute Developmental Therapeutics Program using the NCI-60 human tumor cell line panel at a single concentration of 10 μM. AZT exhibited modest antiproliferative activity, producing a mean growth percentage of 98.27% and demonstrating its greatest activity against leukemia and myeloma cell lines. The CuAZT complex produced a similar mean growth percentage (96.05%) but substantially altered tumor selectivity, increasing the response range from 80.22 to 190.27 percentage units. The most notable finding was the emergence of enhanced melanoma activity. CuAZT produced net cell death in MDA-MB-435 melanoma cells (-61.63% growth) and reduced average melanoma growth from approximately 98.9% to 69.4%. These findings suggest that Cu(II) coordination modifies the biological response profile of AZT primarily through changes in tumor selectivity rather than through a substantial increase in overall potency. The distinctive activity profile of CuAZT supports future mechanistic studies and dose-response evaluation. Because Zidovudine (AZT) is still studied and utilized for specific retrovirus-linked cancers, although it is not a general-use chemotherapy drug for common solid tumors, using the 60 cell line panel provides insight to its efficacy against multiple types of cancer. In addition, our use of Cu(II) to improve the efficacy Taxol, raised the question if Cu(II) could do the same for AZT.

items.title: Accessing Alkyl Linkers for Macrocyclic Peptide Synthesis via Nickel-Mediated Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization
items.abstract: The rise of macrocyclic peptides as a therapeutic modality has exposed gaps in the synthetic chemistry toolbox available for drug discovery teams to rapidly explore diverse linkers for structural optimization. In contrast to the thioether linkers common in peptide leads identified from mRNA display, all-carbon linkers are desirable for imparting solubility and stability, but existing approaches suffer from limited amino acid diversity, incompatibility with solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), stereochemical loss, multistep requirements, or restricted linker placement. We report a Doubly DeAminative Macrocyclization (D2AM) to install alkyl linkers via C(sp3)–C(sp3) bond formation. This method uses pyridinium monomers derived from commercial amino acids that are stable to SPPS for the seamless synthesis of complex macrocyclic and polycyclic peptides with conservation of stereochemistry. This deaminative method is anticipated to accelerate optimization of peptide macrocycle structure in drug discovery.

items.title: Allosteric Control and Glycan Shielding Adaptations in the SARS-CoV-2 Spike from Early to Peak Virulence
items.abstract: The SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein is central to viral infectivity and immune evasion, making it a key target for vaccine and therapeutic design. This trimeric peplomer undergoes dynamic conformational changes, particularly in its Receptor Binding Domain (RBD), which transitions between closed (down) and ACE2-accessible (up) states relative to the rest of the protein, to facilitate host cell entry. Structural understanding of such critical interdomain motions, as well as epitope exposure quantification, is essential for obtaining an effective biochemical handle over this protein and, in turn, exploiting it toward improved immunogen development. Focusing on the early circulating D614G form and the later emerging Delta (B.1.617.2) variant with higher virulence, we performed large-scale molecular dynamics simulations of the soluble form of the Spike in both “down” and “up” conformations of the RBD. Guided by differences in domain-scale fluctuations, we constructed targeted reaction coordinates capturing NTD and RBD rotations and tilting motions, enabling variant-specific structural distinctions to be quantitatively extracted. Conformational landscape mapping and principal component analysis (PCA) reveal a previously uncharacterized dynamic coupling between the NTD and RBD, wherein tilting motions of the NTD are coupled to RBD gating on the neighboring protomer. While several elements of this interdomain coupling are conserved, the Delta variant exhibits a more constrained and functionally optimized RBD-up conformation that favors ACE2 engagement. Concurrently, Delta-specific mutations restructure NTD-local glycans to enhance shielding of the immunogenic supersite, diminishing neutralizing antibody accessibility. Finally, the D950N substitution at the heptad repeat HR1 helix reshapes long-range interactions and alters bending/twisting dynamics of the Spike stalk, likely contributing to both fusion efficiency and immune evasion. Together, these simulations uncover chemically encoded strategies of variant adaptation─through long-range allostery, glycan repositioning, and conformational bias─that shape Spike structure and function. These biochemical and structural insights offer valuable guidance for rational vaccine and therapeutic design against SARS-CoV-2 and emerging variants.

items.title: A Narrative Review on Cholesterol Homeostasis, Lipid Metabolism, and Vitamin D3 in Neurological Disorders
items.abstract: The mammalian brain contains the highest cholesterol concentration, a steroidal lipid essential for neuronal physiology and function. Much evidence reflects the importance of cholesterol’s homeostasis in the central nervous system and how its imbalance causes synaptic dysfunction and facilitates neurodegeneration. Cholesterol impairment may affect the structure and function of neurons, and dysregulation of its homeostasis has been commonly observed across neurodegenerative and neuropsychological disorders, as seen in Alzheimer’s disease (AD), Parkinson’s disease (PD), Huntington’s disease (HD), and schizophrenia (SCZ). Beyond its classical role in calcium and phosphate regulation, Vitamin D3 (VD) has emerged as a promising neuroprotective nutraceutical. This review evaluates current evidence linking VD deficiency to disrupted brain cholesterol homeostasis and discusses how VD may preserve brain cholesterol homeostasis by regulating cholesterol turnover, lipid transport, neurotrophin signaling, and membrane organization in AD, PD, HD, and SCZ.

items.title: Chemical analysis of drug samples as a response to the toxic drug crisis
items.abstract: Nature Reviews Chemistry, Published online: 20 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41570-026-00894-9 People who use drugs face risks associated with the unpredictability of an unregulated illicit market. Drug checking is a stopgap measure in the absence of safer supply. While chemists are adept at identifying molecules in complex mixtures, street drug samples present unique analytical challenges when timely, reliable results are needed to inform harm-reduction decisions.

items.title: Treatment of organophosphorus exposure with 6-alkoxypyridin-3-ol quinone methide precursors able to reactivate and resurrect the cholinesterases

items.abstract: 5-Fluoroindolylmethylene hydrazones were investigated as potential inhibitors of human carbonic anhydrase isoforms hCA I and hCA II through in vitro assays and in silico studies.

items.title: Design, synthesis, and biological evaluation of pyrimidine-based hydrazones as multitarget inhibitors of EGFR, PI3K, AKT1, ERK1, CDK1, and Hsp90 against breast cancer
Targeting Neuropilin-1 with EG00229 Attenuates Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension in a Murine Sugen/Hypoxia Model
items.abstract: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a progressive vasculopathy driven by pulmonary vascular remodeling that leads to right ventricular failure and premature death. Despite improvements with therapies targeting the three canonical vasoactive pathways (nitric oxide, endothelin, and prostacyclin)─including endothelin receptor antagonists, phosphodiesterase type-5 inhibitors, soluble guanylyl cyclase stimulators, and prostacyclin analogues─most patients do not achieve disease remission. This highlights the critical need for disease-modifying approaches that directly target and reverse pathological vascular remodeling. Recent advances, including the approval of the activin-signaling inhibitor sotatercept, suggest the feasibility of strategies that target novel antiremodeling pathways; however, PAH remains incurable for the vast majority. Neuropilin-1 (NRP1) is a multifunctional coreceptor expressed by endothelial cells (ECs) and pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs). The receptor orchestrates intracellular signaling by binding multiple ligands implicated in PAH pathobiology, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-A, transforming growth factor (TGF)-β family members and platelet-derived growth factors (PDGFs), and modulates endothelial junctional stability, permeability and smooth muscle cell migration Here, we show that NRP1 is overexpressed in pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells from patients with PAH and that pharmacological inhibition of NRP1 with the novel small-molecule antagonist EG00229 attenuates hemodynamic and structural features of the disease in the gold-standard Sugen 5416/hypoxia (SuHx) mouse model of PAH. EG00229 reduced right-ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary arterial muscularization without affecting systemic blood pressure or body weight, supporting on-target pulmonary selectivity. These findings identify NRP1 as a tractable therapeutic target with potential to modulate vascular remodeling in PAH.

items.title: Immune and Stromal Barriers to Active Nanoparticle Targeting of Claudin-4 in Tumors
items.abstract: Nanoparticles with targeting ligands can act as “magic bullets” to selectively target tumor cells, a concept that has captivated the drug delivery field for decades. Using cell culture, engineered mouse models, and spatial imaging, we studied how cellular interactions influence targeting of claudin-4 (CLDN4), a key ovarian cancer target. We coupled the C-terminal domain of Clostridium perfringens enterotoxin (cCPE), a high-affinity CLDN4 binder, to ∼60 nm dextran iron oxide nanoworms (CLIO NW) via click chemistry. Targeted NWs had nanomolar affinity for CLDN4 and specifically targeted CLDN4+ cells in culture and 3D spheroids. After systemic injection in mice, targeted NWs exhibited a long plasma half-life. In bilateral CLDN4+/CLDN4– xenograft tumors, targeted NWs accumulated more in CLDN4+ tumors but were also taken up by Kupffer cells in the liver and CD45+ immune cells in both tumors. Repeating the study with anti-CLDN4 IgG-decorated NWs, we again observed high in vitro specificity but low in vivo selectivity, as confirmed by optical and magnetic resonance imaging. Spatial proteomic analysis of tumors showed that NWs mainly accumulate in tumor cells, immune cells, and myofibroblasts, with tumor core cells mostly negative for NWs. Cell stress and metabolic profiles remain unchanged after the uptake. Coculture of CLDN4+ tumor cells and macrophages replicated the limited selectivity of targeted NWs in vivo and suggested that complement opsonization contributes to limited selectivity. Overall, stromal and immune uptake hinder CLDN4 targeting. Future efforts should focus on understanding and inhibiting nanoparticle uptake pathways to develop molecularly targeted nanomedicine.

items.title: Shake It Off: Abl Kinase Regulatory Domain Dynamics Explain Conformational Changes upon Activation
items.abstract: Abl kinase is a major molecular target for chronic myeloid leukemia therapy. Its activity is tightly controlled by its regulatory module, composed of the SH3 and SH2 domains and the SH2–kinase linker. Although the assembled autoinhibited and extended active conformations have been structurally characterized, the molecular pathway connecting these states remains poorly understood. Simulations initiated from the end point structures failed to sample the complete transition, even when Gaussian accelerated molecular dynamics (GaMD) was employed to enhance conformational sampling. To overcome this limitation, we combined multiscale modeling with extensive molecular dynamics simulations and Markov state modeling to reconstruct the Abl disassembly pathway. The resulting kinetic landscape revealed two coupled conformational equilibria: a faster exchange between the canonical assembled state and an intermediate ensemble that captures the initial rotation of the regulatory module, and a slower transition toward the extended state, characterized by migration of the regulatory module atop the kinase domain N-lobe. The assembled ensemble is favored (∼88% of the equilibrium population), with the canonical autoinhibited arrangement alone accounting for approximately 60%, while early disassembly disrupts the E98–K294 and SH3–linker interactions and releases Y226 from its protective interactions, while Y70 remains accessible through the intrinsic dynamics of the SH3 domain. By revealing how these phosphorylation-sensitive residues become accessible during the earliest stages of disassembly, our model provides a mechanistic framework for Abl activation and identifies regulatory interfaces as potential targets for allosteric stabilization of the autoinhibited state.

items.title: Low-Energy Photon-Mediated Skeletal Editing of Indole to Quinazoline via a Nitrogen Insertion Reaction
items.abstract: Skeletal editing enables precise atom-level modification of complex molecules without rebuilding the entire molecular skeleton. Herein, we report a low-energy photoredox-mediated protocol for nitrogen atom insertion into indoles, providing direct access to biologically relevant quinazoline scaffolds without stoichiometric oxidants. Mechanistic studies support a pathway involving singlet-oxygen-mediated oxidation of indoles, followed by ammonia interception of the resulting oxidative cleavage intermediate. The method exhibits broad applicability to indole derivatives and tolerates a diverse range of functional groups. Late-stage skeletal editing of complex molecules and successful scale-up demonstrate their synthetic utility.

items.title: Biocatalytic Carboligation As a Versatile Route to (Rare) monosaccharides
items.abstract: Rare monosaccharides have emerged as valuable building blocks for the chemical manufacturing of pharmaceuticals and food additives. Although numerous biocatalytic strategies have focused on the interconversion of naturally abundant sugars, bottom-up enzymatic synthesis from smaller carbon sources represents an increasingly attractive alternative route that offers high stereochemical control. This review provides a comprehensive overview of the de novo (or bottom-up) enzymatic synthesis of monosaccharides through carbon–carbon bond-forming biocatalysis (i.e., carboligation). We cover aldolases, transaldolases, transketolases, and the recently developed formolases, highlighting their catalytic mechanisms, substrate scopes, stereochemical outcomes, and complementary synthetic capabilities. Representative synthetic routes toward free trioses, tetroses, pentoses, and hexoses (ketoses and aldoses) are systematically and critically analyzed, with attention to reaction efficiency, isolated yields, and cascade integration.
