Significant developments exploiting engineered enzymes, multi-enzyme cascades, whole-cell systems, and hybrid chemoenzymatic processes are discussed, including strategies that directly valorize abundant platform chemicals (e.g., glycerol) and C1 feedstocks such as formaldehyde and carbon dioxide into structurally diverse carbohydrate scaffolds. By focusing on experimentally validated syntheses in which target monosaccharides have often been isolated and quantitatively characterized, this review identifies the current strengths and limitations of bottom-up biocatalytic approaches. Finally, emerging opportunities in enzyme discovery, protein engineering, and integrated catalytic cascades are highlighted, illustrating how advances in carbon–carbon bond-forming biocatalysis are paving the way toward selective and versatile access to rare monosaccharides.

items.title: Polyketide–Nonribosomal Peptide Hybrids from Fusarium sp. with Antifungal Activities
items.abstract: Four unprecedented polyketide–nonribosomal peptide hybrids, fusaridienes A–D (1–4), were obtained from the endophytic fungus Fusarium sp. Compounds 1–4 represented the first reported examples of lucilactaenes bearing a bicyclo[3.2.1]octadiene scaffold. Extensive spectroscopic data analysis, combined with ECD computations and DP4 + probability analysis, led to the establishment of their structures and absolute configurations. Plausible biosynthetic pathways for 1–4 were proposed. Bioactivity evaluation revealed that 7 exhibited superior efficacy against Cryptococcus gattii 3291 compared to fluconazole. Mechanistic studies revealed that 7 exerted antifungal activity by inducing oxidative stress, impairing ribosomal synthesis, suppressing protein production, and attenuating the virulence factors melanin and urease.

items.title: Novel Rho-associated protein kinase (ROCK) inhibitors with favorable vasorelaxant and antihypertensive activities
Design, synthesis, and antiviral evaluation of N-arylacetamide-nicotinonitriles as potential inhibitors of the PA endonuclease domain of influenza a virus
Multiscale Modeling of Virus Capsid Self-Assembly Reveals How Small Molecule Antivirals Can Redirect Assembly Pathways and Products
items.abstract: Controlling the assembly of a virus capsid, a regular complex of hundreds of subunits, has applications for development of antivirals and for development of nanocontainers. Recent work has shown that a class of small molecules called capsid assembly modulators (CAMs) is promising for treating Hepatitis B virus (HBV). CAMs bind to HBV capsid proteins and alter their self-assembly, leading to nonfunctional and malformed structures. The mechanisms by which CAMs alter capsid assembly remain unclear. Here, we use a kinetic Monte Carlo (KMC) model for HBV capsid assembly to simulate how CAMs affect this complex reaction. The model is parametrized from all-atom simulations, resulting in unprecedented correlation between simulation and biochemical and structural observations. Simulations reproduce the effect of CAMs on experimental assembly products and their distributions. By analyzing assembly trajectories, we clarify the roles of thermodynamics and kinetics in determining assembly products, identify assembly mechanisms, and predict the key intermediates that lead to either capsids or malformed structures. Our findings enhance our fundamental understanding of capsid assembly, help advance the development of CAMs as a treatment for HBV and, more broadly, inform efforts to direct self-assembly pathways toward specific products.

items.title: Rational Optimization of a Peptide-Guided Delivery System Enhances Macrophage Targeting and Drug Biodistribution toward Inflammation
items.abstract: Macrophages play a central role in various inflammatory diseases by regulating immune responses through the secretion of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors, making them attractive targets for anti-inflammatory therapies. However, macrophage-modulating strategies often face challenges in the delivery specificity toward inflammatory sites, resulting in the unwanted disruption of normal immune functions. We previously identified a macrophage-targeting peptide, termed CRV. Through binding to retinoid X receptor beta (RXRΒ), CRV conjugation may navigate drugs more selectively to the inflammatory sites upon intravenous (IV) injection and thus improve their therapeutic efficacy and safety profile. Here, we optimized this CRV-guided delivery system from multiple aspects. To improve the macrophage targeting, we performed iterative molecular docking-based optimization of CRV sequence. This study identified a variant, termed CRH, with a substantially higher predicted binding affinity to RXRΒ. We further validated that compared to CRV, CRH possesses a greater affinity for RXRΒ protein and macrophage cells in vitro and exhibits a higher accumulation in inflammatory sites after IV injection in vivo. Using dexamethasone (DEX) as an example of anti-inflammatory drugs, we also investigated the impact of other components in this RXRΒ-targeted delivery system on drug biodistribution. Collectively, we report here an optimized, peptide-guided delivery system that may provide a more desirable drug biodistribution profile toward inflammatory sites and thus may serve as the foundation for a more selective delivery of anti-inflammation therapies.

items.title: Discovery of Potent and Selective Quinazoline-Based LATS1/2 Inhibitors Promoting Hepatic Regeneration
items.abstract: Therapeutic acceleration of endogenous liver regeneration remains a considerable unmet need for patients with acute or chronic liver injury. Among the pathways that coordinate regenerative responses, the Hippo pathway and its main components LATS1/2 kinases play a critical role by limiting YAP-dependent transcriptional programs associated with regeneration. Pharmacological inhibition of LATS1/2 thus represents a strategy to activate hepatic YAP signaling and promote tissue repair. Herein, we report the discovery of quinazoline-based LATS1/2 inhibitors derived from VT-02956 (1). Structure−activity relationship studies identified compound 24, a single-digit nanomolar LATS1/2 inhibitor with improved cellular YAP activation and metabolic stability. Compound 24 showed favorable kinase selectivity (S(35) = 0.04) and improved pharmacokinetics. In a partial hepatectomy mouse model, intraperitoneal administration of 24 activated YAP signaling, as evidenced by the upregulation of Cyr61 and Ankrd1, and significantly enhanced hepatocyte proliferation. These findings establish a medicinal chemistry foundation for developing LATS1/2 inhibitors as therapeutic agents for hepatic regeneration.

items.title: Isotopic Labeling of the Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor Binimetinib with Fluorine-18 and Preclinical Evaluation
items.abstract: The Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK signaling pathway is involved in numerous cancers. Monitoring its overactivation by PET imaging remains challenging, yet it holds significant potential for personalized diagnostics. Here, we report the fluorine-18 isotopic radiolabeling of binimetinib, an FDA-approved specific allosteric MEK1/2 inhibitor, for the treatment of BRAF-positive melanoma. The inherent structure of binimetinib makes its radiolabeling a strong challenge, addressed by evaluating seven precursors using a simplified model compound. A fully automated, four-step, one-pot radiosynthesis afforded [18F]binimetinib with a 9 ± 5% radiochemical yield after 100 min with >95% radiochemical purity. In vitro evaluation of [18F]binimetinib demonstrated specific uptake in H358 cells with activated Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK. PET imaging of an H358 xenograft mouse model revealed promising tumor uptake at 4 h post-injection with 1.96 ± 0.51 % ID.cm−3 in the tumor. This study provides insight into the in vivo pharmacokinetic profile derived from PET imaging of [18F]binimetinib and its potential for investigating MEK target availability in tumors.

items.title: Machine Learning-Assisted Image Analysis of Sub-visible Particles in Biologics Drug Products: A Comparative Study Using Micro-Flow Imaging and FlowCam
items.abstract: Sub-visible particles (SvPs) in parenteral drug products present patient safety and product quality risks. While Micro-Flow Imaging (MFI) and FlowCam are established for SvP enumeration and morphological assessments, inferring particle identity and origin from images alone remains challenging due to diverse inherent, intrinsic, and extrinsic sources, as well as stress-induced changes in particle populations. This study developed and evaluated a deep-learning workflow that integrates transfer-learning feature extraction with anomaly detection and similarity search to improve ground truth label quality and supervised classification to differentiate proteinaceous and non-proteinaceous SvPs. A comprehensive panel of SvP types relevant to biologicsincluding protein aggregates generated under thermal, pH, mixing, and agitation stresses; fatty acids; silicone oil droplets; elastomeric stopper particles; glass lamellae; and fibrous contaminantswas imaged on both FlowCam and MFI. Subject matter experts curated labels, and features extracted via VGG16/ResNet50 informed anomaly detection for label/quality control. Three classifiers (a baseline CNN, DenseNet121, and YOLOv8) were evaluated and benchmarked. Across models built with particle images of varying sizes (5−10 μm, 10−25 μm, >15 μm, and >25 μm), YOLOv8 achieved the highest performance (FlowCam: accuracy 0.973; MFI: accuracy 0.918), with strong precision/recall and specificity, outperforming both the baseline CNN and DenseNet121. Clustering analyses further revealed separations between protein vs non-protein SvPs and showed the model’s potential ability to distinguish stress-specific protein aggregates across multiple molecules, suggesting potential utility in root-cause analysis during development and manufacturing. This comparative, cross-platform study highlights the value of modern classification architectures as a complementary SvP identification tool to confirmatory spectroscopies (e.g., Raman/FTIR), thereby improving process understanding within biologics development.

items.title: Microwave-Assisted Carbonylative Sonogashira Coupling of Phenylalanine and Peptide Derivatives: An Alkynone Platform for Heterocycles and Environment-Sensitive Fluorophores
items.abstract: We report a microwave-assisted carbonylative Sonogashira coupling that installs alkynones into phenylalanine and peptide derivatives. The method supports bioconjugation, late-stage macrocyclization, diverse terminal alkynes, and varied peptide sequences while preserving stereochemical integrity. The resulting alkynones enable divergent access to pyrimidine, pyrazole, and isoxazole derivatives and display environmentally responsive photophysical behavior and metal–ion interactions.

items.title: Development of Second Generation Thieno[2,3- d ]pyrimidin-4-one Derivatives as Positive Allosteric Modulators of the N -Methyl- d -Aspartate Receptor
items.abstract: The N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) is a ligated-gated cation channel that mediates excitatory synaptic transmission in the central nervous system. These receptors are involved in important brain functions and have been implicated in many neuropathological conditions. Four GluN2 subunits assemble with GluN1 to produce a series of NMDAR subtypes that are expressed in different subpopulations of neurons at different times. Among the GluN2 subunits, the GluN2D-containing NMDARs are highly expressed in inhibitory interneurons, which are key targets for drug development. Positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) have been proposed to be useful in several neuropsychiatric indications, including schizophrenia and depression. We have previously discovered EU 1622-240, a novel GluN2B/C/D-biased PAM with favorable oral bioavailability, CNS exposure, and anxiolytic activity in rodents. However, it was a P-gp inhibitor, cleared rapidly, and poorly absorbed in vivo. Through an extensive SAR, we now present EU 1622-287 with improved solubility, oral bioavailability, brain exposure, and anxiolytic effects.

items.title: QM/MM Simulations Reveal Differences in Hydrolysis Mechanisms of Ertapenem and Faropenem in L1 Metallo-β-Lactamase Leading to Different Product Binding Modes
items.abstract: L1, a class B3 metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) from Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, efficiently hydrolyzes most β-lactam antibiotics and evades β-lactamase inhibitors, both clinically available and those in late-stage trials targeting other MBLs. Detailed understanding of the L1 mechanism is necessary to design effective inhibitors. Building on our previous quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics (QM/MM) study of L1catalyzed hydrolysis of the penem antibiotic faropenem, we here investigate hydrolysis of a 1β-methyl carbapenem (ertapenem) using MM and enhanced sampling QM/MM MD simulations at the DFTB3 level, comparing the two mechanisms to understand the distinct product binding modes observed crystallographically. The geometry of the transition state for the first, amide bond cleavage, reaction step is similar for both substrates. However, differences are apparent in the subsequent proton transfer step, corresponding to the different binding modes observed crystallographically for the respective products. For faropenem, a bulk water molecule enters the active site, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product via rotation about the C5–C6 bond and protonation at position C2. For ertapenem, the metal-bridging hydroxide is the proton source, and the equivalent rotation is associated with a relatively high barrier. Instead, the more favorable rotation of the C6-carboxyl enables protonation at C2, yielding the (2S )-imine-∆1 product in a distinct binding mode. Long-timescale MM MD simulations indicate rapid dissociation of the ertapenem-derived imine, compared to the faropenem-derived species, from the L1 active site, offering insight into the relative stability of these binding modes. These data reveal how carbapenem and MBL structure influence hydrolysis pathways, and may inform rational MBL inhibitor design.

items.title: Late-Stage Diversification of Peptides into Unsaturated Amides and Thioesters via Phosphine–Cyclopropenone Chemistry on Solid Phase
items.abstract: Herein, we disclose a phosphine-catalyzed cyclopropenone activation strategy for the late-stage functionalization (LSF) of resin-bound amino acids and peptides. The method, established to be fully compatible with solid-phase peptide synthesis (SPPS), enables efficient on-resin N-terminal amine modification of diverse oligopeptides as well as Lys and Cys side-chain functionalization in peptides, affording the corresponding complex aryl-α,β-unsaturated amide and thioester products with exclusive E selectivity in yields up to 97%, which are otherwise challenging to synthesize. The transformation, proceeding under mild conditions, is suitable for both Rink amide and 2-CTC resins. This approach advances phosphine chemistry in SPPS and establishes cyclopropenone activation as an adaptable platform for on-resin peptide diversification to contain α,β-unsaturated amides, known for targeted covalent inhibition of receptors.

items.title: Two-carbon annulation of primary amines to azetidines
items.abstract: Azetidines are valuable motifs in medicinal chemistry, yet their broader use is constrained by a lack of general, concise methods for preparing N–H azetidines from simple feedstocks. Here, we report a direct two-carbon annulation of unprotected primary alkylamines that provides α-mono- and α,α-disubstituted azetidines. Dual photoredox and hydrogen-atomtransfer catalysis enables α-C–H alkylation with vinylsulfonium reagents to generate γ-amino sulfonium intermediates, which undergo intramolecular SN2 cyclization to forge the fourmembered ring without protecting groups or prefunctionalization. Low-temperature continuous flow is critical for overriding the innate N-centered reactivity of primary amines and suppressing rapid N-alkylation by the vinylsulfonium reagent. The method uses commercially available building blocks, tolerates a range of functional groups, and provides streamlined access to azetidines that are otherwise challenging to prepare. Successful kilogram-scale translation, underpinned by process-safety assessment, demonstrates that the low-temperature flow strategy is transferable beyond discovery scale.

items.title: Piezocatalytic Sulfonation Enables Nongenetic Competition Therapy for Colorectal Cancer
items.abstract: Irreversible post-translational modifications provide a potential means to impose persistent changes in protein function, yet their controlled generation inside living cells remains challenging. Here, we develop an ultrasound-responsive potassium sodium niobate–gold (KNN@Au) piezoelectric nanoheterojunction functionalized with hyaluronic acid (KNN@Au-HA) to enable in situ terminal protein sulfonation. Under ultrasound excitation, the dynamic modulation of KNN polarization generates a piezo-potential that facilitates interfacial charge separation and electron transfer, promoting the single-electron reduction of O2 to •O2–. Meanwhile, Au–S coordination positions thiol substrates in close proximity to the catalytic surface, facilitating the subsequent multistep oxidation of cysteine thiols to the terminal −SO3H state. Using this platform, we identify ribosomal protein RPL32 as a functionally relevant sulfonation target and resolve sulfonation at Cys96 by mass spectrometry. This modification disrupts ribosomal proteostasis, induces NRF2 nuclear translocation and stress signaling, and converts colorectal cancer cells into a competitive “loser” state that undergoes neighbor-dependent apoptotic elimination. In HCT116 xenograft-bearing mice, ultrasound-activated KNN@Au-HA suppresses colorectal tumor growth; analysis of patient-derived single-cell transcriptomic data reveals RPL32 upregulation as a hallmark of the malignant “winner” state, establishing a functional match between this competition therapy and colorectal cancer. Together, these findings demonstrate that piezocatalytic protein modification can chemically reprogram cellular competitive fitness without genome editing, providing a proof of concept for nongenetic competition therapy against cancer.

items.title: Coordination chemistry-driven structure-activity relationships in hydrazide- and Hydrazone-based metal complexes for anti-infective applications
Shortest IZ Motif-Driven Assembly of SARS-CoV-2 HR1 Peptides Yields a Potent Fusion Inhibitor
Divergent activation of the RXFP1 relaxin receptor by protein and small-molecule agonists
items.abstract: The relaxin receptor RXFP1 is a therapeutic target owing to its potential benefits in the treatment of fibrosis and heart failure. Protein and small-molecule agonists are currently in midstage clinical trials for various forms of heart disease. In this work, we present three cryo–electron microscopy structures of RXFP1: ligand-free, bound to the native agonist relaxin-2, and bound to the small-molecule drug candidate AZD5462. These structures reveal that relaxin-2 engages the receptor’s ectodomain, whereas AZD5462 binds to the transmembrane domain. Together with hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry, we show that relaxin-2 induces reorganization of the linker domain into a helical secondary structure. By contrast, AZD5462 stabilizes an active conformation through a distinct set of conformational rearrangements. Altogether, our findings define divergent activation mechanisms for protein and small-molecule agonists of RXFP1.

items.title: A thalamo-amygdalar circuit drives female vulnerability to chronic pain after early-life stress
items.abstract: Childhood adversity increases the risk of chronic pain and anxiety later in life, particularly in women, yet the neural mechanisms linking early-life stress to adult vulnerability remain elusive. Here, we show that social isolation and nerve injury interact to amplify activity-dependent synaptic gain and anticipatory recruitment of the paraventricular thalamus-to–central amygdala pathway in female, but not male, mice. This female-specific circuit sensitization enhances mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance behaviors in adulthood. Chemogenetic pathway inhibition selectively rescued these behaviors when stress and injury co-occurred, whereas sustained and phasic pathway activation triggered mechanical hypersensitivity and avoidance, respectively. Together, these findings uncovered a latent thalamo-amygdalar synaptic gain state that is unmasked by a subsequent injury and transforms early-life stress into female-specific vulnerability to chronic pain and anxiety-like avoidance.

items.title: Balancing redox-mediated cytotoxicity and catalysis in natural product biosynthesis
items.abstract: Redox-mediated chemistry is central to both the biosynthesis and cytotoxicity of many natural products, yet how microbes balance these processes remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a conserved mechanism that coordinates three redox-mediated processes in secondary metabolite biosynthesis: self-protection, prevention of substrate degradation, and late-stage biosynthesis. Using the antitumor antibiotic doxorubicin as a model system, we show that the vicinal oxygen chelate (VOC) protein DnrV prevents reactive oxygen species formation and substrate degradation while promoting P450 catalysis. We expand this paradigm to a conserved family of VOC-fold proteins, redox-associated cytotoxin-binding proteins (REACT), found across bacteria, fungi, and plants. REACT represents a multifunctional protein class that balances antibiotic assembly, self-protection, and prevention of metabolite destruction, providing a foundational understanding of production of redox-active natural products.

items.title: Quaternary carbon–guided carbocation cascade rearrangement to enantioenriched polycycles
items.abstract: Polycyclic frameworks are prevalent in natural products and bioactive molecules, yet their efficient enantioselective synthesis remains a longstanding challenge. Carbocation cascade cyclization is a textbook reaction that has transformed the synthesis of fused polycycles, but extending this strategy to bridged architectures requires precise control over highly reactive carbocation intermediates while overcoming the intrinsic energetic barrier of transannular cyclization. Herein, we report a quaternary-carbon-guided carbocation cascade rearrangement platform that enables enantioselective and divergent assembly of complex polycyclic architectures from readily available substrates. An enantioenriched quaternary center, installed via transition-metal-catalyzed allylation, serves as a temporary structural linchpin in an acid-triggered cationic cascade rearrangement process, forming multiple bonds and chiral centers in a single step. In combination with pre-embedded quaternary centers, this strategy provides bicyclic and bridged polycyclic frameworks bearing multiple stereocenters with high enantioselectivity.

items.title: The Asymmetric Total Synthesis and Biological Evaluation of Dibenzylbutyrolactone Lignan Analogs
items.abstract: The asymmetric synthesis of two naturally occurring, and four non‐naturally occurring dibenzylbutyrolactone lignans is reported. The synthesis utilizes both primary and secondary lignin‐derived xylochemicals as starting materials. Following the synthesis of the racemic 3‐arylmethylbutyrolactone core via a radical cyclization and deracemisation, a subsequent diastereoselective alkylation of this lactone was carried out to afford both (−)‐matairesinol, (−)‐enterolactone, and both enantiomers of four related analogs thereof in moderate to high yields, high diastereoselectivities (>20:1 dr ) and enantioselectivities of up to 97% ee . The cytotoxic and anti‐inflammatory activities of the non‐naturally occurring lignan analogs are analyzed, and the results of this biological evaluation demonstrate the potential of these analogs as anti‐inflammatory agents.

items.title: Gram-Scale Synthesis of the Opiate Alkaloids Mitragynine and Speciociliatine
items.abstract: Several indole alkaloids isolated from the tropical Rubiaceae plant Mitragyna speciosa Korth. exhibit potent μ-opioid receptor-mediated analgesic activity, making these alkaloids and their derivatives promising lead compounds for the discovery of centrally acting analgesics. Herein, we report an enantioselective and convergent total synthesis of the representative Mitragyna indole alkaloids mitragynine and speciociliatine. Starting from commercially available 4-methoxyindole and 1,3-propanediol, mitragynine was synthesized in 13 steps with an overall yield of 15%, enabling gram-scale production while minimizing purification operations throughout the synthetic sequence. The route features a syn-selective organocatalytic Michael addition, a kinetically controlled Pictet−Spengler reaction, and a Shvo’s catalyst-mediated C3 epimerization. Notably, this work constitutes the first total synthesis of speciociliatine and provides a practical synthetic platform for the preparation and biological evaluation of Mitragyna alkaloid derivatives.

items.title: DeepChem-DEL: An Open-Source Framework for Reproducible DEL Modeling and Benchmarking
items.abstract: DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) allow screening of extremely large chemical spaces by tagging compounds with DNA barcodes. Machine learning (ML) techniques have enabled the extraction of meaningful chemical patterns from noisy, target-specific DEL binding data. However, existing tools for DEL machine learning (DEL-ML) remain fragmented, which limits systematic construction and reproducibility of modeling pipelines. Moreover, this fragmentation hinders integration of new models, such as chemical foundation models, into DEL workflows alongside classical approaches. To address these challenges in DEL modeling, we introduce DeepChem-DEL, an open-source suite of reproducible ML workflows for DEL modeling built on the DeepChem ecosystem. DeepChem-DEL integrates (i) a configurable denoising pipeline with (ii) modular DeepChem workflows for enrichment prediction, hit identification, and benchmarking across diverse model classes, including chemical foundation models enabled through extensions to the open-source ChemBERTa-3 framework. We evaluate DeepChem-DEL on the KinDEL and BELKA data sets, reproducing key baselines and enabling direct comparison across model classes. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging chemical foundation models yields performance competitive with, and in several cases exceeding, previously explored approaches such as graph convolutional networks and random forest models. Together, these results demonstrate that DeepChem-DEL is a scalable and extensible platform for DEL-ML, while highlighting the potential of chemical foundation models for improved DEL modeling and prioritization.

items.title: Stepwise Proximity Labeling With a Switchable Organophotocatalyst
items.abstract: Photoinducible proximity labeling (PL) using photocatalysts offers high spatiotemporal resolution for profiling protein–protein interactions (PPIs). Conventional approaches require genetic installation of a tag to tether the photocatalyst to a protein of interest (POI), which may perturb native protein function and cause artificial labeling. Ligand‐directed delivery of photocatalysts to native POIs has emerged as a tag‐free alternative; however, this strategy suffers from nonspecific labeling by unbound catalysts and an inherent washing dilemma, where insufficient washing leads to background labeling while excessive washing disrupts ligand binding. These limitations have severely restricted tag‐free and ligand‐directed PPI profiling. Herein, we report a switchable photoinducible PL strategy based on a nitrobenzoxadiazole (NBD) unit that becomes catalytically active only after covalent conjugation to a POI. This approach consists of a two‐step process: introduction of an N ‐NBD moiety into the POI using a catalytically inactive O ‐NBD unit, followed by light‐induced PL catalyzed by N ‐NBD. N ‐methyl luminol and 1‐methyl‐4‐arylurazole were identified as labeling reagents selectively activated by N ‐NBD. Targeting mitochondrial voltage‐dependent anion channel (VDAC) enabled selective labeling and proteomic identification of mitochondrial proteins. This switchable PL method circumvents the washing dilemma, suppresses nonspecific labeling, and enables tag‐free proteomic analysis with improved spatial selectivity.

items.title: Organobismuth(III) Thiabismine Derivatives as Tunable Metal-Based Antimicrobial and Antitrypanosomal Scaffolds
Ionic and bicontinuous mesoporous carbon nitride with multilevel structures for continuous tandem photosynthesis of value-added chemicals
items.abstract: An amphiphilic ionic bicontinuous mesoporous carbon nitride enables simultaneous photocatalytic co-production of H2O2 and tandem C–H activation/C–N cyclization at the oil-water interface. By repurposing a sacrificial agent into a high-value pharmaceutical intermediate (BzlM), this dual-functional catalyst sustains co-production in a continuous-flow reactor for over 200 hours, offering a generalizable strategy for sustainable biphasic chemical synthesis.

items.title: Bicyclo[2.1.1]hexanes as saturated bioisosteres of meta-benzene
Corrigendum to “Bifunctional inhibitors of β-lactamases and ferroptosis: Design, synthesis and anti-gram-negative bacterial infection evaluation” [Eur. J. Med. Chem. 316 (2026) 119048]
Conformational Plasticity of Orthosteric Pocket Enables the Discovery of a Novel PAD4-Selective Inhibitor
items.abstract: Peptidyl-arginine deiminase (PAD) family enzymes are pivotal enzymes that catalyze the citrullination of arginine in substrate proteins. Elevated levels of citrullinated proteins are tightly linked to the incidence of rheumatoid arthritis, neurodegenerative diseases, and cancers, thus highlighting PAD enzymes as important therapeutic targets. Although several PAD isozyme-selective and non-selective small molecule inhibitors have been reported over the last decade, it remains important to identify distinct ligands that may offer differentiated therapeutic potential or selectivity. Herein, we present a PAD4-selective inhibitor identified through a structure-based virtual screen, which binds to a distinct site from known inhibitors. Biochemical and biophysical characterizations show that the inhibitor is selective for PAD4 over PAD1/PAD2/PAD3 via targeting the orthosteric site preferably at low calcium concentrations. A co-crystal structure of the inhibitor-bound PAD4 shows that the inhibitor binds to an unprecedented pocket near the catalytic site present at low calcium concentrations and stabilizes the catalytically inactive conformation. Owing to its distinctive binding site, this inhibitor series is designated as “Orthosteric B inhibitors”. Structural analysis suggests a unique conformational plasticity of the PAD4 catalytic module, which may help rationalize the PAD4 selectivity of Orthosteric B inhibitors. Further structure-based drug design and computational approaches enabled optimization of the hit to afford a potent PAD4 inhibitor capable of blocking PAD4-mediated protein citrullination in human neutrophils.

items.title: Synthesis of a Selective Orexin 1 Receptor Antagonist: First Scale-Up Campaign Following In-Licensing
items.abstract: Herein, we report the synthesis of 29.2 kg of the selective orexin 1 receptor antagonist C4X3256 monohydrate via a convergent 10-stage synthetic route. (S)-2-(Methylamino)-1-[5-(trifluoromethyl)-2-pyrazinylamino]propane was synthesized in 5 stages from l-alaninamide·HCl and isolated as the crystalline HCl salt. 6-Methyl-3-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine-2-carboxylic acid was synthesized in 4 stages from 5-bromo-2-methylpyridine and isolated as the hemidiisopropylethylamine salt. The two advanced intermediates were combined in the final stage using T3P as a coupling reagent.

items.title: Synthesis of a Selective Orexin 1 Receptor Antagonist: Development of a Manufacturing Process─Part 2
items.abstract: In campaign 1, 75.3 kg of (S)-2-(methylamino)-1-[5-(trifluoromethyl)-2-pyrazinylamino]propane hydrochloride salt was prepared in two stages from (S)-2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine d-tartaric acid salt. The first stage was the alkylation of 2-chloro-5-(trifluoromethyl)pyrazine. The second stage was the removal of the benzyl protecting group by hydrogenolysis. In campaign 2, 251 kg of (S)-2-(methylamino)-1-[5-(trifluoromethyl)-2-pyrazinylamino]propane hydrochloride salt was produced, this time starting from the d-mandelic acid salt of (S)-2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine. Investigations into alternative routes of synthesis for (S)-2-(methylamino)-1-[5-(trifluoromethyl)-2-pyrazinylamino]propane identified two options: one via (5R)-5-methyl-3-[5-(trifluoromethyl)pyrazin-2-yl]-1,2λ6,3-oxathiazolidin-2,2-dione and the other via (S)-2-(N-benzyloxycarbonyl-N-methylamino)propionitrile.

items.title: Synthesis of a Selective Orexin 1 Receptor Antagonist: Development of a Manufacturing Process─Part 3
items.abstract: In campaign 1, 124.3 kg of 2-methyl-5-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine N-oxide (8) was prepared in 2 stages from 5-bromo-2-methylpyridine. The first stage was a regioselective copper-catalyzed Ullmann reaction using 1H-1,2,3-triazole. The second stage was an oxidation with peracetic acid to form the corresponding pyridine N-oxide. In campaign 2, 223.8 kg of 2-methyl-5-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine N-oxide (8) was prepared. An alternative palladium-catalyzed Buchwald−Hartwig approach using Me4tBuXPhos as a ligand was developed but not scaled up. 2-Methyl-5-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine N-oxide (8) is a key intermediate in the synthesis of the orexin 1 receptor antagonist C4X3256.

items.title: Synthesis of a Selective Orexin 1 Receptor Antagonist: Development of a Manufacturing Process–Part 1
items.abstract: In campaign 1, 103.9 kg of (S)-2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine d-tartaric acid salt (4) was prepared in 3 stages from l-alaninamide·HCl. The Stage 2 reaction, the reductive amination of (S)-2-benzylaminopropionamide (2) with aqueous formalin using H2, Pd/C, and THF as solvent, proved to be nonrobust. Ahead of campaign 2, the Stage 2 and 3 processes were redeveloped to provide a higher yielding and more robust set of reaction conditions. The key change was to conduct the reductive amination of (S)-2-benzylaminopropionamide (2) with aqueous formalin using NaBH4 in MeOH as solvent while maintaining a constant pH (pH = 8.5) by the addition of acetic acid. In campaign 2, (S)-2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine was isolated as the d-mandelic acid salt. A total of 373 kg of (S)-2-(N-benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine d-mandelic acid salt was produced in high yield and excellent quality. (S)-2-(N-Benzyl-N-methylamino)-1-propanamine is a key intermediate in the synthesis of the orexin 1 receptor antagonist C4X3256.

items.title: Synthesis of a Selective Orexin 1 Receptor Antagonist: Development of a Manufacturing Process─Part 4
items.abstract: In campaign 1, 97.75 kg of the orexin 1 receptor antagonist C4X3256 (1) was prepared in 3 stages from 2-methyl-5-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine N-oxide (8). In the first stage, the nitrile group was introduced using trimethylsilyl cyanide and benzoyl chloride. In the second stage, the nitrile was hydrolyzed to the carboxylic acid using aqueous NaOH and the acid isolated by crystallization as the hemidiisopropylethylamine salt. In the third stage, 6-methyl-3-(2H-1,2,3-triazol-2-yl)pyridine-2-carboxylic acid (10) was coupled with the previously prepared amine (S)-2-(methylamino)-1-[5-(trifluoromethyl)-2-pyrazinylamino]propane hydrochloride salt (6) using T3P to produce C4X3256. In campaign 2, a combination of 1-ethyl-3-(3-(dimethylamino)propyl)carbodiimide hydrochloride and 2-hydroxypyridine N-oxide was used in place of T3P as the coupling agent to produce 293.5 kg of C4X3256 (1).

items.title: Dual Transition-Metal Electrocatalysis for Allylic Fluoroalkylation of Unactivated Alkenes Using Fluoroalkyl Carboxylic Acids
items.abstract: Allylic fluoroalkylation enables the facile incorporation of medicinally valuable fluoroalkyl motifs into abundant, structurally varied alkenes. Existing strategies, however, predominantly rely on expensive and atom-inefficient fluoroalkylating reagents or stoichiometric redox chemicals for the generation of productive fluoroalkylating intermediates, which severely limit their scalability and practical utility. Here, we report a Fe/Co dual transition-metal electrocatalytic strategy that merges photoelectrochemically driven iron-catalyzed decarboxylation with cobalt-mediated dehydrogenation to achieve allylic C–H fluoroalkylation of unactivated alkenes. Readily accessible fluoroalkyl carboxylic acids serve as the fluoroalkyl sources, without the use of exogenous redox chemicals or the pre-functionalization of fluoroalkyl carboxylic acids. This catalytic system tolerates a wide spectrum of functional groups and smoothly converts unactivated alkenes into synthetically versatile allylic fluoroalkylated products with good efficiency. Its synthetic utility has been demonstrated through the late-stage derivatization of alkenes derived from bioactive molecules.

items.title: Linker Optimization Enhances Wash-Free Imaging of Escherichia coli Dihydrofolate Reductase-Tagged Proteins
items.abstract: Protein tagging based on the trimethoprim (TMP)–Escherichia coli dihydrofolate reductase (eDHFR) pair enables selective fluorescence imaging through high-affinity, noncovalent ligand binding. Here, we systematically investigated how linker structure, linker amide chemistry, and fluorophore identity influence the performance of TMP-based fluorescent probes. A library of 15 probes based on TMR, MaP555, and JF526 was synthesized and evaluated in vitro and in cells. Linker optimization markedly affected probe lipophilicity, intracellular labeling efficiency, image contrast, and labeling kinetics. Increasing linker hydrophobicity generally promoted efficient intracellular labeling, whereas excessive hydrophobicity increased intracellular background fluorescence. Amide N-methylation emerged as an effective strategy for improving cellular probe performance and was incorporated into the best-performing probes in all three fluorophore series. In vitro fluorogenicity was not necessarily predictive of live-cell imaging performance. The optimized probes enabled efficient wash-free imaging of diverse eDHFR-tagged intracellular structures. These findings provide practical design principles for improving TMP-based fluorescent probes and may guide the development of probes for other protein-tagging systems.

items.title: BALLROOM A and S–A Benchmark Created Automatically from Structurally Resolved Pockets with Homogeneously Measured Affinities/Series
items.abstract: Computational methods for virtual screening and lead optimization are benchmarked on specifically designed data sets to predict compound potency. Here we present a workflow and two resulting new benchmark data sets, BALLROOM A and BALLROOM S, from combining PDB and ChEMBL data. Due to high data quality standards, the formation of molecule pairs measured under the same conditions only, and avoiding pairs with close to equal potency, we achieve a reliable data collection for physics-based bioactivity prediction based on protein–ligand complex structures. When testing state-of-the-art scoring functions for docking, no classical method statistically outperforms a simple molecular-weight-based prediction, consistent with previous studies such as D3R. While challenging for physics-based methods, the prediction task can be easily addressed by simple nearest-neigbor scorers showing that the benchmark cannot be used for machine learing based scoring functions due to significant train-test inference.

items.title: Discovery of an RNF126-Dependent Polθ Degrader Exhibiting In Vivo Activity in an HR-Deficient Tumor Model
items.abstract: DNA polymerase theta (Polθ), a multidomain DNA repair enzyme, has emerged as a promising synthetic-lethal target in homologous recombination (HR)-deficient tumors, yet current inhibitors directed at either its helicase or polymerase domain may not fully suppress the functions of the intact protein. Here, we report PR-6, a RNF126-dependent Polθ degrader identified through comparative degrader screening and structural optimization. In BRCA1-deficient MDA-MB-436 cells, PR-6 induced, concentration- and time-dependent Polθ degradation via an RNF126- and ubiquitin-proteasome-dependent mechanism. Compared with the Polθ helicase inhibitor AB25583 under the tested cellular conditions, PR-6 exhibited greater antiproliferative activity and induced more pronounced DNA damage and apoptosis. Moreover, PR-6 synergized with Olaparib in vitro and markedly potentiated its antitumor efficacy in an MDA-MB-436 xenograft model without overt toxicity. These findings support PR-6 as the first degrader probe for interrogating Polθ biology and provide proof of concept for Polθ degradation as a complementary strategy in HR-deficient tumors.

items.title: Scaffold Hopping from Quinazoline to Tetrahydropyrido[3,4- d ]pyrimidine: Enhancing the Potency and Selectivity of HIV-1 Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors
items.abstract: In this work, a series of tetrahydropyrido[3,4-d]pyrimidine derivatives were rationally designed as HIV-1 non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors via scaffold modification. Most compounds demonstrated promising potency against wild-type HIV-1 (IIIB) and clinically relevant mutants. Notably, 10p showed the strongest activity against HIV-1 IIIB, L100I, K103N, Y188C, Y188L, and E138K (EC50 = 2.4−16.5 nM). Importantly, 10p maintained potent efficacy against F227L/V106A (EC50 = 12.3 nM) and K103N/Y181C (EC50 = 21.7 nM). In vitro assessment revealed that the metabolic clearance rate of 10p in human liver microsomes was moderately lower than that of rilpivirine. Additionally, 10p showed a low potential for CYP-mediated drug interactions and had a negligible inhibitory effect on the hERG potassium channel. In the acute oral toxicity study in mice, no adverse effects were observed at a dose of up to 2000 mg/kg. These findings identify 10p as a promising lead compound for further development.

items.title: Toward Distributed Robustness in Resistance-Aware Lead Optimization
items.abstract: Drug resistance often enters lead optimization after a compound has been chosen. We define distributed robustness as redistributing predicted binding support away from predefined mutable contacts while retaining wild-type feasibility and panel coverage. ResistAgent separates site-level and observed combination-level liabilities, diagnoses their structural effects, and compares a matched-budget robust objective with an average-affinity comparator. Across 10 EGFR pairs, the median reduction in hotspot dependence, ΔDep (naive − robust; positive values favor the robust objective), was +0.042; across 9 valid HIV-RT pairs, it was +0.026. Panel passing was preserved but not improved: both objectives passed in every valid pair. ABL1 yielded 2/4 pairs without a corresponding robustness gain. The objective changes the dependence organization and candidate selection. Provider comparisons, ranking benchmarks, and explicit-water contact descriptors are reported alongside the primary endpoint.

items.title: What Does Generalizable AI in Drug Discovery Really Mean?
items.abstract: Machine learning models increasingly contribute to drug discovery, but their utility depends on performing reliably in their intended deployment setting. Although model generalization is invoked frequently, the drug discovery community lacks a shared vocabulary for how models actually achieve transferability beyond their training data. We argue that achieving generalization requires examining how a model’s inductive bias interacts with its training data to shape the notion of similarity it learns. Without a bias that makes relevant recurring relationships easier to learn as opposed to incidental correlations, models exploit dataset-specific shortcuts. These shortcuts yield high benchmark performance but fail in prospective applications. We therefore propose evaluation principles tailored to a model’s architecture, using diagnostic controls and train−test splits that distinguish transferable learning from the retrieval of familiar training data. This Perspective shows how representational choices shape failure modes across pose-dependent, pose-independent, and foundation model paradigms, and provides a practical framework to help researchers expose shortcuts and interpret predictions.

items.title: Iodine(III)-Enabled Photocatalytic Skeletal Editing of Carbocyclic Amides Via Radical–Polar Crossover
items.abstract: Skeletal editing enables the direct modification of molecular frameworks through atom insertion, deletion, or replacement. However, catalytic nitrogen insertion into ring-strained C–C bonds remains challenging, particularly for the synthesis of saturated diazacycles from readily available carbocyclic precursors. Here, we report an iodine(III)-enabled photocatalytic strategy for the skeletal editing of carbocyclic amides through a radical–polar crossover pathway. The method enables formal 2N insertion into bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane (BCP) amides, affording 2,3-diazabicyclo[3.1.1]heptanes, a bridge-constrained scaffold with potential as a diazine bioisostere. Tuning the electronic properties of the acetoxybenziodoxole (BI-OAc) additive further enables the synthesis of benzodiazepines, tetrahydropyrazoles, and hexahydropyridazines from different carbocyclic amides. Mechanistic studies, including the isolation of a cyclization intermediate, support a radical–polar crossover pathway in which the BI-OAc additive is proposed to facilitate productive cyclization, while suppressing linear byproduct formation. The method has been demonstrated across 72 substrates, including gram-scale synthesis and late-stage modification of bioactive molecules. It also accommodates carbon-based coupling partners, enabling formal two-carbon insertion for complementary skeletal editing of carbocycles. This strategy provides a direct approach to nitrogen-rich, three-dimensional molecular frameworks.

items.title: Self-Oxygenated Radionuclide Delivery System for Synergistic Sensitization of Tumor Chemotherapy and Radionuclide Therapy
items.abstract: Radionuclide therapy is a clinically effective approach for precision cancer treatment. However, its efficacy is severely compromised by the hypoxic tumor microenvironment and intrinsic DNA self-repair mechanisms. Moreover, a single treatment modality is often insufficient to eradicate tumors. To address these challenges, we designed and constructed a multifunctional dendritic mesoporous silica (dendritic mesoporous silica nanoparticles)-based delivery system co-loaded with the chemotherapeutic agent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) and catalase (CAT). The delivery system surface was modified with human serum albumin and hyaluronic acid (HA), followed by radiolabeling with the radionuclide 131I to enable tumor-targeted delivery, hypoxia alleviation, and synergistic radiotherapy−chemotherapy effects. This radionuclide delivery system exhibits excellent radiolabeling stability, biocompatibility, and SPECT imaging properties. It leverages CAT to efficiently catalyze the decomposition of endogenous H2O2 in the tumor microenvironment to generate O2, thereby significantly relieving tumor hypoxia. HA modification confers superior active tumor-targeting capability, while sustained release of 5-FU under acidic conditions at the tumor site effectively inhibits DNA replication. Both in vitro and in vivo experiments demonstrate that this system synergistically enhances the efficacy of 131I brachytherapy and 5-FU chemotherapy, leading to marked tumor growth inhibition with low systemic toxicity. Overall, this study overcomes the hypoxic tumor barrier and achieves synergistic targeted therapy combined with chemoradiotherapy, offering a novel strategy for effective and low-toxicity clinical treatment of solid tumors.

items.title: Targeting FSP1 to induce ferroptosis: advances in small-molecule inhibitors, degraders and their structure-activity relationships
Discovery of HC9591, a Selective Macrocyclic EGFR C797S Inhibitor with Brain Exposure in Rats
Photoinduced On-DNA C–S Coupling Enables Access to α-Sulfenylated Carbonyl Scaffolds
items.abstract: A mild, transition-metal-free photoinduced on-DNA C–S coupling strategy provides direct access to α-sulfenylated carbonyl scaffolds. Operating as a telescoped one-pot protocol, it overcomes previous synthetic limitations for the preparation of these DNA-conjugated motifs. Notably, the method enables late-stage diversification of cereblon-binding glutarimide scaffolds used in IMiD drugs and CRBN-recruiting PROTACs directly on DNA barcodes, enabling efficient DNA-encoded libraries (DELs) synthesis.

items.title: Prospective Execution of a Generative Peptide Design Workflow at the Keap1–Nrf2 Interface
items.abstract: Deep-learning tools for peptide design and structure prediction are increasingly combined into screening workflows, but at the Keap1–Nrf2 interface such work has rarely progressed beyond computational characterization. We report a case study in which an initial-round workflow built from publicly available components─ProteinMPNN, Chai-1, PLIP, and HADDOCK3─was fixed before any experimental data were obtained and its complete prioritized output was carried to synthesis and measurement: 530,299 unique sequences from seven Nrf2-derived backbones were reduced to 5,118 by sequence filtering and to 28 by structure-based filtering, and all 28 were synthesized and assayed alongside 16 analogues and the native Nrf2 12-mer, giving 45 measured peptides. One design, a 12-mer carrying an ENGE variant of the ETGE motif, inhibited the interaction with an apparent IC50 of 120 nM under the assay conditions used, whereas the 14 resampled analogues satisfying the same structural criteria showed low inhibition, indicating that within this workflow the structure-based steps acted as filters for structural plausibility rather than as predictors of activity. Because the set was measured in full and the intermediate sequence sets were retained, we also report how the composition of the surviving population changed across the cascade; the original workflow data are released.

items.title: Total Synthesis of (+)-Sulfadixiamycin B via Site-Selective Twofold Csp2–H Amination
items.abstract: Indolosesquiterpenoid alkaloids constitute a structurally complex and biologically significant class of natural products, exemplified by the sulfadixiamycins, which feature rare N–S–C and C–S–C linkages and exhibit notable antimicrobial activity. Despite their unique molecular architecture and promising biological properties, no total synthesis of the sulfadixiamycin family has been reported to date. Herein, we report the first total synthesis of sulfadixiamycin B through a convergent strategy. The synthesis features the efficient assembly of a dapsone-derived biaryl sulfone fragment and an abietane-derived tricyclic boronate ester by Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling, followed by a late-stage Pd-catalyzed oxidative C–N bond forming reaction to construct the pentacyclic carbazole framework with excellent regioselectivity. This concise synthetic route provides efficient access to sulfadixiamycin B and establishes a platform for the synthesis of related sulfur-containing indolosesquiterpenoids, enabling future biological evaluation and structure–activity relationship studies.

items.title: Brønsted-Acid-Catalyzed Direct Deoxygenation of Benzylic and Tertiary Alcohols with Hydrosilanes Enabled by 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol
items.abstract: Brønsted-acid-catalyzed deoxygenation of benzylic and tertiary alcohols into hydrocarbons with hydrosilanes in a HFIP/dichloromethane solvent system has been developed. In contrast to classical Barton–McCombie-type radical protocols, the present method proceeds at 25 °C using a simple Brønsted acid catalyst and near-stoichiometric amounts of hydrosilane, significantly improving reagent economy. A wide range of electronically and sterically diverse substrates were efficiently transformed, with broad tolerance toward acid-sensitive functional groups, unprotected phenols, and additional hydroxy groups, enabling late-stage deoxygenation of structurally complex bioactive molecules.

items.title: ezABFE: An Easy-to-Use Workflow for Absolute Binding Free Energy Calculations
items.abstract: Absolute binding free energy (ABFE) calculations can evaluate chemically diverse ligands, but their complex workflows remain challenging for nonexpert users and prone to errors. Here, we present ezABFE, an easy-to-use Python workflow for automated ABFE calculations within the AMBER ecosystem. ezABFE minimizes manual intervention in system preparation, representative-structure selection, Boresch restraint atom selection, simulation setup, free-energy estimation, and graphical analysis. The workflow employs both MBAR and TI for alchemical free-energy estimation and additionally provides MM-GBSA and optional MM-PBSA end-point calculations. Benchmarking across T4 lysozyme L99A, BRD4(1), CDK8, and the theophylline-binding RNA aptamer shows good overall agreement with experimentally derived binding free energies and comparable performance of MBAR and TI. Additional tests demonstrate that appropriate Boresch restraint atom selection is important for simulation stability and binding free-energy accuracy, and that ligand partial-charge models and the HMR/4 fs simulation protocol can influence calculated affinities, although the limited comparisons do not support general conclusions regarding either factor. The computationally inexpensive end-point methods also retain practical value for ligand ranking. Overall, ezABFE provides an accessible, automated workflow for reproducible ABFE calculations with improved throughput across diverse receptor systems, including nucleic acid receptors.

items.title: Remodeling of Norbornadiene with HB(C6F5)2 Affords Access to Cobalt-Bound 1-Boraindene Heterocycles
items.abstract: Synthetic routes to monobenzannulated boroles (1-boraindenes) remain relatively rare. Here we show that reaction of [Cp*Co(NBD)] (Cp* = C5Me5–, NBD = norbornadiene) with Piers’ borane, (HB(C6F5)2)2, affords a mixture of two Cp*Co complexes, each incorporating a π-coordinated 1-boraindene ligand. For one of the observed isomers, C–C bond cleavage results in the formation of a ring-opened, hydrogenated ethylcyclopentenyl substituent. This transformation demonstrates a ring-opening/functionalization sequence in which the typically spectator NBD ligand is converted into a skeletal synthon, enabling metal-mediated construction of a cobalt-bound 1-boraindene framework.

items.title: Electrochemistry Goes Mainstream: Applications in Modern Total Synthesis
items.abstract: For more than a century, synthetic organic electrochemistry has held out the promise of using electrons and holes─the universe’s cheapest and most tunable redox reagents─to orchestrate bond construction and functional-group interconversion with unparalleled precision and sustainability. Yet, for decades, its role in total synthesis remained peripheral, usually invoked when all else failed or as an alternative to reactions with a chemical counterpart. Why did a technique whose industrial pedigree includes multi-ton processes at BASF languish at the margins of academic complex molecule synthesis until the past ten years? The reasons are as familiar as they are frustrating: bespoke equipment, a steep learning curve, and the comforting (if often illusory) notion that “chemical reagents can do that, too.” Our laboratory’s entry into the field was pragmatically rather than philosophically driven. During the total synthesis of dixiamycin, exhaustive screening of chemical oxidants failed to forge the requisite N–N bond; constant-potential electrolysis succeeded cleanly. That single, necessity-driven success in 2014 marked the beginning of a deliberate campaign to move electrochemistry from workaround to strategic centerpiece. What followed was a convergence of two enabling developments: (1) the commercialization of standardized, user-friendly potentiostats that removed the engineering barrier, and (2) the invention of fundamentally novel reactivity─most notably, electrochemical radical cross-couplings─that unlocked intermolecular C–C bond formations between late-stage, densely functionalized fragments in manners hardly accessible using classic two-electron methods. In this Account, we illustrate how these advances have rippled across every major natural-product class and bond type. Strategic functionalizations such as decarboxylative borylations (jawsamycin) and site-selective C–H oxidations (valencene, sclareolide, mitrephorone) now deliver gram-scale intermediates with minimal concession steps. Electrochemical C–N and C–O constructions have powered protecting-group-sparing routes to teleocidins, dragocins, and bipolarolides. The real paradigm shift, however, lies in intermolecular radical cross-couplings. C(sp2)–C(sp3) unions have enabled modular, scalable entries to polyene cores (progesterone, celastrol, isosteviol, vitamin D analogues) and complex macrocycles (bipinnatin J, micitide 982), while doubly decarboxylative C(sp3)–C(sp3) couplings have delivered 15 natural products, including polyrhacitide A and PF1163A, both stemming from a single, inexpensive building block with ligand-controlled diastereoselectivity. Most strikingly, two sequential electrochemical couplings furnished over a gram of the intricate antibiotic nonthmicin, tolerating epoxides and free diols that would have derailed any conventional tactic. Electrochemistry has therefore ceased to be a niche curiosity and has become standard practice in our laboratory (64 syntheses to date)─and, increasingly, in the broader community. It offers an orthogonal retrosynthetic logic that maximizes convergence, minimizes redox fluctuations and protecting groups, and leverages inexpensive electricity rather than stoichiometric metals or pyrophoric reagents. The field now stands at an inflection point: practical paired electrolyses, direct reductive transformations, and mediator systems capable of engaging ever more complex substrates are within reach. For the synthetic chemist who has contemplated a stubborn redox problem or a chemoselectivity impasse, electrochemistry is no longer a last resort─it is an obvious tool to consider employing.

items.title: Halogen‐Dependent Regulation of the Thyroid Hormone Transporter by Antipsychotic Drugs and Their Analogues
items.abstract: Antipsychotic drugs are primarily used to manage psychosis and other psychotic disorders. Their main mechanism of action involves blocking dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, and they remain important for the treatment for schizophrenia. In this paper, we describe an unusual property of several commonly used antipsychotic drugs and their analogues for their ability to modulate the thyroid hormone transporter system. Specifically, these compounds significantly increase the protein expression of monocarboxylate transporter 8 (MCT8), a key transporter responsible for carrying thyroid hormones across the plasma membrane in a variety of cell lines. Our findings indicate that the presence of halogen substituents plays a critical role in promoting the MCT8 upregulation. Furthermore, the magnitude of this effect is dependent on the nature of the halogen atom, with iodine‐containing phenothiazine derivatives exhibiting the strongest induction of MCT8 expression. The increased transporter expression was accompanied by enhanced cellular uptake of MCT8‐selective fluorescent probes, confirming functional activity. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first example of halogen‐dependent regulation of protein expression in mammalian cells.

items.title: Universal Transfer Reagents for the Synthesis of Carbon‐Labeled Methyl, Fluoromethyl, and Difluoromethyl Motifs
items.abstract: The preparation of 13 C‐ and 14 C‐labeled difluoromethyl compounds remains a major challenge despite the growing importance of the CF 2 H group in medicinal chemistry. Here, we report a practical and sustainable solution based on carbon‐labeled sulfoximines readily prepared from primary isotopic sources. These stable reagents act as versatile C1‐transfer agents and provide access not only to difluoromethyl derivatives, but also to cyclopropanes, epoxides, and monofluoromethyl compounds. The strategy enables the efficient synthesis of valuable labeled building blocks and pharmaceutical motifs under mild conditions. By unifying multiple labeling transformations around a common precursor class, this work significantly broadens the scope of carbon‐isotope chemistry for life‐science applications.

items.title: Pairwise learning of cyclic peptide membrane permeability on a matched-molecular-pair graph
items.abstract: Cyclic peptides are a promising drug scaffold that can target proteins considered undruggable by small molecules, but their poor membrane permeability limits further application. Deep learning has been used to lower the wet-lab burden of finding cell-permeable peptides. Most existing models are trained on measurements curated from many publications and predict a single peptide’s permeability directly. That formulation ignores systematic measurement differences between publications, and it does not answer the actual question drug development asks: not whether a peptide is permeable, but which modification would make a given lead peptide more permeable. Here we introduce CycPeptMMP, which learns the permeability difference within a matched molecular pair (denoted as pair mode) instead of a single peptide’s value (denoted as single mode). Conventional molecular pairing approaches do not apply to cyclic peptides, so we constructed a graph of matched molecular pairs over the four modification types commonly used to improve permeability, organizing 5,674 peptides across seven publication sources. We trained both single and pair modes on five graph neural network backbones across 10 random splits. Pair mode performs better on sources with fewer than 1,000 peptides except Wang, whose peptides often lack a close analogue. Pair mode’s advantage is greatest for the closest analogues differing by a single modification. Single mode is preferable for sources with more than 1,000 peptides. We also implemented a censored loss to retain peptides with clamped measurements in the regression. For pairs involving those peptides, pair mode is more accurate when predicting which one in the pair is more permeable. Taken together, we provide a framework for comparing single and pair mode within each source, and show where pair mode is worth using.

items.title: Carbonylative Assembly of Strained Dispirocyclic Architectures from [1.1.1]Propellane
items.abstract: Herein, we report a strain-release carbonylation of [1.1.1]propellane that enables direct access to methylenecyclobutane dispirocyclic diketones. By combining the exceptional strain energy of [1.1.1]propellane with the unique reactivity of carbon monoxide, the process achieves simultaneous skeletal reorganization, carbonyl incorporation, and dispirocycle construction in a single operation. The resulting dispiro diketones further serve as versatile platform molecules for skeletal editing and molecular diversification.

items.title: Ionic routers encode GPCR activation state on both sides of the membrane
items.abstract: In both class A and B1 G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), certain charged residues exchange one salt-bridge partner for another between the active and inactive states: each binds one oppositely charged residue in the active state and a different one in the inactive state, with neither partner bound in both. Their ionic bonds are rerouted rather than lost, and neither state leaves them free. Such residues are called ionic routers [1]. We report the complete set of ionic routers the structural record deposited in the Protein Data Bank supports across class A and B1 receptors, and the first evidence in any GPCR that the arrangement reaches the extracellular face. Our earlier screen fixed the 4.0 angstrom salt-bridge cutoff in advance [1]. Here the screen is given only the pattern of contacts a router must show, and the cutoff is solved for. Enumerating every charged three-residue arrangement that 762 deposited structures of the 61 class A and B1 receptors with structures in both activation states can evaluate reduces 7,266 directed triples to 211 in which a pivot is opposed in charge by both partners. Two meet the definition, both required bonds placed above majority occupancy by a 95 percent interval: on activation, rhodopsin E247 (6.30x30) exchanges R135 (3.50x50) for K231 (5.66x66), releasing the contact the ionic lock literature describes, and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) E408 (8.49x49) exchanges R348 (6.37x37) for R176 (2.46x46). These are the two reported previously, recovered here without that criterion: a test of the earlier ranking measure, not a repetition of it. The two-router answer holds across a contiguous window from 3.75 to 4.25 angstroms, with the conventional 4.0 interior to it. Below the window only rhodopsin survives. Each router sits on the most deeply sampled receptor in its class, rhodopsin of 56 in class A and GLP-1R of 5 in class B1. Only 13 of 61 receptors carry four or more scorable structures on any arrangement’s weaker arm, the minimum at which selection is possible. Router discovery is record-limited.

items.title: Fluorination-Enabled Stereochemical Editing of Sialic Acid
items.abstract: Sialic acids trace the evolutionary arc of contemporary glycoscience and continue to provide inspiration for drug discovery. However, harnessing the potential of sialic acids in a therapeutic context is contingent on unlocking chemical space and devising strategies that allow the venerable C9 framework to be selectively modified in an operationally simple manner. Enabled by judicious C(sp3)-F installation at C3, the configuration of this center can serve as a lever to facilitate a series of structural editing events in a programmable fashion. This is exemplified by the regiodiversity of amide cyclization: (R)-configuration → 5-membered ring formation; (S)configuration → 7-membered ring formation with concomitant acetyl migration, to access bridged-bicyclic scaffolds that are reminiscent of naturally occurring sialic acids. Importantly, this [CH2 → CHF] isosteric replacement enables selective modification at C2 (glycosylation), C4 (epimerization) and C5 (N-deacetylation). Given the ubiquity of C3 fluorinated sialic acids in chemical biology and biomedicine, it is envisaged that this conceptual framework will expedite chemical space exploration.

items.title: N-Alkyl Cyanopyridinium Salts as Modular N-Terminal Cysteine Warheads for Site-Specific Bioconjugation and Living Cell Engineering
items.abstract: Site-specific protein modification is central to chemical biology and to therapeutic development. Stringent control over a single site delivers homogeneous conjugates and underpins the synthetic engineering of proteins and cells, which demands streamlined and reliable chemistry. An N-terminal cysteine (NCys) represents a unique canonical amino acid handle easily incorporated into peptides, proteins, and cells, yet its use remains underexplored. Building on 2-cyanobenzothiazole (CBT), we show that quaternizing the ring nitrogen of an otherwise sluggish cyanopyridine gives N-alkyl 4-cyanopyridinium salts (4CP+) with markedly improved kinetics, aqueous solubility, synthetic accessibility, and modularity. Moreover, 4CP+ reacts selectively with NCys to deliver a wide range of biochemical reporters and tumor-receptor ligands to peptides and proteins, enabling modular assembly of functional conjugates, as exemplified by smallmolecule–protein hybrid T cell engagers. We further developed a divinyl 4CP+ that rebridges native disulfides while retaining the nitrile as a latent handle for late-stage payload installation, extending NCys chemistry to modular synthesis of homogeneous therapeutic conjugates from cyclic peptides to off-theshelf monoclonal antibodies. We also demonstrated that a genetically encoded NCys serves as a minimal conjugation tag, which, paired with 4CP+ reagents, achieves site-specific protein labeling on live cell surfaces, including a natural killer cell line, opening up cell-conjugation applications.

items.title: Heteroleptic Cu(I)-Photosensitizer-Catalyzed Molecular Oxygen Activation for Selective Oxidation of Sulfides to Sulfoxides
items.abstract: The selective oxidation of sulfides to sulfoxides represents a cornerstone transformation in organic chemistry, yet conventional methods rely on stoichiometric toxic oxidants and harsh conditions. While photocatalytic alternatives including noble-metal complexes and organic dyes suffer from inadequate chemoselectivity or poor photostability. Herein, we report a visible-light-driven aerobic oxidation of sulfides to sulfoxides catalyzed by a heteroleptic Cu(I) complex using molecular oxygen as the sole oxidant. Heteroleptic copper(I) complex operates under open-air conditions with blue LED irradiation, requiring no additives or stoichiometric oxidants. The protocol exhibits outstanding chemoselectivity and broad functional group tolerance, alongside high atom economy and a low E-factor. The quenching experiments and spectroscopic studies reveal a dual-pathway mechanism involving both superoxide anions and singlet oxygen as reactive oxygen species. The modular nature of heteroleptic Cu(I) complexes allows fine-tuning of photophysical properties, including favorable redox potentials and long-lived triplet states, which promote efficient ROS generation. Synthetic utility is demonstrated through the late-stage oxidation of drug molecules, including medapsol, albendazole sulfoxide precursors, valproic acid and gemfibrozil derivatives, underscoring its practical relevance in medicinal chemistry. Collectively, this work establishes a robust, sustainable, and broadly applicable platform for selective sulfoxide synthesis, highlighting the potential of heteroleptic Cu(I) photocatalysts in green oxidation chemistry.

items.title: 6,7-Difunctionalized 2-Azanorbornanes from a Bench-Stable Aziridinium Salt: Scope, Limitations, and Multigram Synthesis
items.abstract: 2-Azanorbornanes (2-azabicyclo[2.2.1]heptanes) are present in approved drugs, yet practical methods for their functionalization at C6 and C7 are scarce. Herein, we report a two-cycle approach to 6,7difunctionalized 2-azanorbornanes from a single aziridinium salt. The salt is prepared in two steps from cyclopentadiene on a scale of up to 300 g per run. It is a bench-stable crystalline solid that can be stored and handled as a regular reagent. In the first cycle, O-, N-, S-, F-, C-, and P-nucleophiles open the aziridinium ring at C6 with complete regio- and stereoselectivity. In the second cycle, the bromine at C7 is replaced by azide, cyanide, or fluoride with retention of configuration, or removed reductively. The approach provided conformationally restricted amino acids, diamines, and fluorinated building blocks for medicinal chemistry on a gram to multigram scale.

items.title: Drug-resistance phenotypes in FGFR deep mutational scanning are carried by a single-residue positional statistic that transfers across FGFR1–3 and weakens in FGFR4
items.abstract: Motivation: Drug-resistance mutations are a clinically central but poorly predicted phenotype: pathogenicity predictors trained on disease labels misrank them, and our recent benchmark of five static predictor families (AlphaMissense, FoldX stability, FoldX interaction energy, ThermoMPNN-D and AutoDock Vina) showed that biophysical scores predict FGFR resistance poorly. Whether supervised recalibration on functional deep mutational scanning (DMS) labels can repair this, and what feature class carries the signal, remains untested. Results: Using the DMS of the FGFR1–4 kinase domains (Tangermann et al. 2026; 7,522 unique variants) under leave-one-subtype-out validation, raw AlphaMissense correlates negatively with the resistance score in every subtype (ρ = −0.46 to −0.65), and on the binary task models built on biophysical scores reach AUROC 0.54–0.74 and never exceed the position-based model (scores 0.56–0.64 vs position 0.73–0.87 on the complete-case subset, n = 5,135). On the continuous score, a one-parameter sign flip remains the strongest recalibration. The signal is instead carried by an aligned-position prior: a parameter-free lookup of resistance rates at each aligned kinase-domain coordinate, transferred from the training subtypes. The lookup matches or exceeds a gradient-boosted model (AUROC 0.88, 0.89, 0.84, 0.70 for FGFR1–4), is strongly resistance-skewed (pure-resistance 0.86, 0.84, 0.84, 0.61; pure-activating 0.62, 0.60, 0.42, 0.46), peaks at single-residue resolution, sits 0.16–0.30 above the strongest clinical-hotspot baseline, and reaches AUPRC 0.31–0.48 with 37–63% precision in the top 50; a two-stage blend that resolves within-site ordering raises this to 36–64% with a tie-free ranking at no AUROC cost. The prior transfers across drugs (pemigatinib → futibatinib, 0.74–0.83) and across FGFR1–3, weakening for FGFR4. Conclusion: FGFR resistance phenotypes are recoverable from a homology-transferred positional label statistic — a lookup table, not a fitted model; the lookup alone recovers the discrimination, and a within-site score ranker refines the top of the list without adding discrimination. The statistic is specific to resistance, contains information beyond known clinical hotspots, and transfers across drugs within the FGFR inhibitor class.

items.title: Elucidation of a ThiF-Like Enzyme-Mediated Biosynthetic Pathway for Scalemic N -Acyl Amides with Antiangiogenic Activity
items.abstract: Chirality is a defining feature of natural products, yet the biosynthetic origins of scalemic metabolites remain poorly understood, particularly in bacteria. Here, we report the discovery of stereochemically diversified N-acyl amides from the marine bacterium Pseudovibrio denitrificans. We show that these metabolites, existing in racemic, scalemic, and enantiopure forms, are synthesized via a stepwise transformation-and-trapping pathway mediated by PdfB, a standalone ThiF-family adenylyltransferase. PdfB generates a transient, electrophilic oxazolone intermediate that undergoes spontaneous racemization, acting as a synthetic hub for nucleophilic attack. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these N-acyl amides exhibit potent stereospecific antiangiogenic activity by enhancing von Hippel-Lindau protein (pVHL)-associated proteasomal degradation of hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF)-1α. This study expands the functional repertoire of ThiF-like enzymes and establishes a new conceptual framework for stereochemical diversification in bacterial metabolism, connecting microbial scalemization with the regulation of host hypoxia signaling.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Generating Drug-like Molecules: A Taxonomy of Methods and Evaluation Strategies
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used for de novo small-molecule design, but the practical and translational utility of generated candidates depends on the configuration of the entire discovery workflow rather than on generative model architecture alone. This review adopts a workflow-based perspective on generative molecular design, tracing the process from existing molecular data sets, preprocessing and representation, to molecule generation, conditioning, candidate prioritization, evaluation, and iterative refinement. It examines how generative AI model families, constraints, and predictive oracles interact within this pipeline, and evaluates generated candidates using intrinsic metrics, computational assessments, and experimental and translational evidence. Active learning, computational and experimental feedback, and human expert input are further discussed as mechanisms for closed-loop refinement. Across these stages, we identify data construction and representation choices, oracle quality, evaluation protocols, and the availability of informative feedback as major determinants of how model performance should be interpreted and whether generated structures progress toward biologically and translationally meaningful candidates, with selected examples. In conclusion, reliable generative drug discovery requires coordinated design across the entire workflow rather than isolated advances in individual components.

items.title: From De Novo Molecular Design to Experimentally Validated Protein-Protein Interaction Modulators
items.abstract: Identifying bioactive small molecules requires balancing target affinity with physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties compatible with drug development. This is particularly challenging in the development of small-molecule modulators of protein–protein interactions (PPIs) due to the structural complexity of protein interfaces. Here, we developed an integrated workflow combining de novo molecular design with similarity-guided identification of existing compounds from public chemical libraries. We applied this strategy to neuronal calcium sensor-1 (NCS-1), a calcium-binding protein whose interactions with multiple partners regulate synaptic function, making it an attractive target for modulating neuronal signaling. REINVENT4-based molecular generation incorporated predicted binding to the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice, synthetic accessibility, and CNS-relevant ADMET properties, including blood–brain barrier permeability. Generated structures guided the selection of commercially available analogues. Experimental validation supported the effectiveness of this AI-guided strategy: 11 of the 12 tested compounds bound NCS-1, including 5 with micromolar affinities. In situ protein–protein interaction assays further confirmed the modulatory activity of selected compounds, identifying, to our knowledge, the first small-molecule enhancers of the NCS-1/cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1R) interaction. CB1R is an attractive pharmacological target implicated in neuronal signaling, whose activity is regulated by NCS-1. High-resolution crystal structures revealed how these modulators engage the NCS-1 hydrophobic crevice, providing structural insights into ligand recognition and suggesting a mechanism of action. These findings connect generative molecular design with experimentally accessible NCS-1 ligands and provide chemical tools and structural insights for investigating NCS-1-dependent regulation of CB1R.

items.title: New Carboxyl-Functionalized Heptamethine Cyanines as Phototherapeutic Agents for Colorectal Cancer: Tunable Targeting Enables Dual-Mechanism to Induce Cancer Cell Death
TH-CADD: An Integrated High-Performance Computing Platform for Large-Scale Computer-Aided Drug Discovery
items.abstract: The growing scale of chemical libraries and the increasing complexity of biological targets have made high-throughput computer-aided drug design (CADD) an essential component of modern drug discovery.
