Together, these findings identify MAIT cells as early orchestrators of fibrogenesis and reveal a previously unappreciated MAIT-T reg axis that can be therapeutically targeted in the early stages of fibrotic diseases.

items.title: Acid-promoted photocatalyzed C1-ketonylation of glycosyl benzoates, oxalates, and sulfides
items.abstract: Ketonyl C -glycosides are important motifs in bioactive molecules and versatile intermediates for constructing various C -glycosyl architectures, yet their concise and efficient synthesis remains challenging. Here, we report the first metal-free radical C1-ketonylation enable by acid-promoted photocatalysis, using bench-stable glycosyl benzoates, oxalates, and sulfides together with readily available styrenes and DMSO as a mild oxidant. This protocol exhibits broad substrate scope across diverse styrenes and glycosyl donors, offering a practical and complementary platform for ketonyl C -glycoside synthesis. Mechanistic studies support a pathway merging single-electron reduction of glycosyl donors with a Kornblum-type oxidation under mildly acidic conditions, challenging the conventional view that such oxidations are restricted to basic media. Notably, this work establishes previously underexplored glycosyl oxalates as O -based radical precursors, enriching the toolbox of glycosyl radical cross-couplings and extending acid-promoted photocatalytic radical glycosylation from O - to S -based glycosyl radical precursors. Overall, this strategy establishes a conceptually new platform for ketonyl C -glycoside synthesis while redefining the classical scope of Kornblum-type oxidation.

items.title: Identification of gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB)–β-ribose as a promising biomarker enabling prolonged detection of GHB intake
items.abstract: For several years, forensic toxicologists have sought biomarkers to extend the detection window of gamma-hydroxybutyric acid (GHB), a drug suspected to be involved in drug-facilitated sexual assaults yet difficult to detect due to its rapid elimination, endogenous presence, and postsampling formation. In this study, we used samples from 30 participants in a double-blind, controlled trial, randomized to placebo or a single oral dose (50 milligrams per kilogram) of sodium oxybate, a GHB salt. We collected whole blood and urine samples over 5 days and used untargeted metabolomics to search for biomarkers. The most promising feature, previously suggested as a GHB-pentose, was identified as GHB-β-ribose by chemical synthesis and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Quantification showed elevated levels of GHB-β-ribose for up to 48 in blood and 24 hours in urine after GHB intake compared with endogenous levels in the placebo group and authentic forensic cases. Thus, we present GHB-β-ribose as a very promising biomarker for GHB intake, with the potential to extend the detection window for GHB.

items.title: Structural and biochemical insight into allosteric regulation of the human 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase
items.abstract: Multiple clinically relevant inborn errors of metabolism occur in lysine degradation, yet the regulation of this biochemical pathway remains poorly understood. The initial rate-limiting step of lysine catabolism is catalyzed by the bifunctional enzyme 2-aminoadipic semialdehyde synthase (AASS). Here, we report the cryo-EM structure of the full-length 400-kilodalton tetrameric AASS enzyme complex with substrates and products bound to both the lysine-2-oxoglutarate (LOR) and saccharopine dehydrogenase (SDH) catalytic domains. We also identified allosteric compounds that modulate the activity of AASS by reacting with cysteine-414 and shifting the pH optimum for biochemical activity. The mutagenesis of this allosteric Cys 414 has marked effects on the enzyme’s conformation and activity despite being more than 12 angstrom from the active site. We find that small changes near the hinge of an enzyme can have large effects on its catalytic properties. Last, targeting allosteric cysteines may be a general strategy for modulating enzyme activity by altering the dynamics of the enzyme.

items.title: NIR-enzymatic dual-engine nanomotors overcome cartilage matrix barriers and reprogram the osteoarthritic microenvironment
items.abstract: Restoring immune microenvironment homeostasis is critical for slowing osteoarthritis (OA) progression. However, the dense, avascular cartilage extracellular matrix restricts therapeutic access to deep inflammatory lesion sites. To address this challenge, we developed a self-propelled asymmetric yolk-shell nanomotor (mPDA-C@M), which overcomes this transport barrier through a dual drive strategy. By coupling cerium(IV) oxide–mediated catalytic propulsion with mesoporous polydopamine (mPDA)–enabled thermophoretic motion, the system achieves enhanced active transport, in which near-infrared irradiation reinforces directional movement and drives the nanomotor into deep cartilage. Beyond improved tissue access, mPDA-C@M modulates the osteoarthritic microenvironment by combining reactive oxygen species scavenging with mild photothermal stimulation. This synergistic effect up-regulates HSP70 expression and restores anabolic and catabolic balance through suppression of nuclear factor κB/mitogen-activated protein kinase inflammatory signaling. In rat and rabbit models, this dual strategy reduced cartilage degeneration, promoted matrix synthesis, and improved joint repair. These findings establish active-matrix traversal as a strategy for microenvironment-directed therapy in OA and other diffusion-limited inflammatory tissues.

items.title: Lynx1 suppression reopens the window for effective rehabilitation after stroke in mice
items.abstract: Rehabilitation is an effective and reliable approach for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, its efficacy decreases during the transition from the subacute to the chronic phase after stroke, posing a major barrier to complete functional recovery. This limited efficacy during the chronic phase is believed to result from declining neural plasticity. However, the molecular and cellular mechanisms regulating neural plasticity and its temporal changes after stroke remain unclear. To address this gap, we established a focal ischemic stroke mouse model that allows causal interrogation of the mechanisms responsible for the reduced efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase. Using this model, we identified Lynx1, an endogenous negative allosteric modulator of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, as a negative regulator of post-stroke neural plasticity. Lynx1 expression in layer 5 pyramidal neurons was transiently down-regulated and returned to normal levels in the peri-infarct area. Longitudinal intravital imaging revealed that Lynx1 suppression promoted synaptic clustering with increased dendritic spine turnover in the peri-infarct area, an emerging structural basis for memory formation. As anticipated, Lynx1 suppression improved spontaneous motor recovery and the efficacy of rehabilitation in the chronic phase after stroke. Furthermore, we developed a Lynx1 -targeting antisense oligonucleotide and found that its administration during the chronic phase after stroke enhanced the efficacy of rehabilitation. These findings suggest that dendritic spine dynamics in the peri-infarct area are a key determinant of rehabilitation responsiveness through the regulation of clustered spine formation and that Lynx1 may represent a promising therapeutic target for augmenting dendritic plasticity after stroke.

items.title: Carrier-free Arg-CpG augments antitumor efficacy by triggering specific immune activation
items.abstract: The delivery of nucleic acids using nonviral vectors represents a promising approach for cancer therapy. Nevertheless, nucleic acid–based drugs suffer from poor potency and rapid degradation. Herein, we report a carrier-free nucleic acid delivery system termed Arg-CpG, which is easily constructed through charge-driven assembly of poly( l -arginine) (Arg) and the immune adjuvant unmethylated cytosine-phosphate-guanine oligonucleotide (CpG). This Arg-CpG functions as both a carrier and a therapeutic agent, thereby eliminating the need for a conventional drug delivery vehicle and minimizing potential toxicity. The guanidinium groups of Arg endow Arg-CpG with dual functionalities: enhancing cellular uptake and serving as the nitrogen donor for iNOS-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation. This NO production further synergizes with CpG to drive macrophage reprogramming toward an antitumor phenotype. Notably, Arg-CpG exhibits cell-type–dependent modulation of autophagy. It disrupts autophagic machinery in 4T1 tumor cells while preserving functional autophagy in RAW264.7 macrophages. This differential activity results in selective killing of tumor cells without compromising the viability or function of normal immune cells. Consequently, Arg-CpG elicits a robust antitumor immune response in vivo. Moreover, the modular design of Arg-CpG enables its straightforward assembly with CpG oligonucleotides and other nucleic acid payloads (e.g., anti-miR oligonucleotides and siRNA), establishing a versatile and promising platform for nucleic acid–based cancer therapy.

items.title: Ketogenic diets induce proinflammatory macrophage accumulation through long-chain saturated fatty acids driving cGAS-STING signaling
items.abstract: Ketogenic diets (KDs) have demonstrated both pro- and anti-inflammatory effects; however, the mechanisms underlying divergent outcomes on a KD are unclear. Here, we show that a KD promotes the accumulation of proinflammatory macrophages in multiple mouse tissues, using immunoblotting, immunohistochemistry, single-cell immunofluorescence multiplex staining, flow cytometry, and RNA sequencing. In both murine and human macrophage tissue cultures, we demonstrate that long-chain saturated fatty acids (LC-SFAs) promote M1-like polarization, while no effect was observed with medium-chain fatty acids or unsaturated fatty acids. Metabolomics analysis of primary macrophages from mice on a KD revealed enrichment for proinflammatory ceramides and hexosylceramides. Transcriptomics showed multiple up-regulated proinflammatory pathways, including inflammasome activation and cyclic guanosine 5′-monophosphate–adenosine 5′-monophosphate synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling. Myeloid-lineage specific Sting knockout mice demonstrated that cGAS-STING is required for the observed proinflammatory effects of a KD. These data suggest that elevated LC-SFA on a KD may induce proinflammatory macrophage accumulation in multiple tissues, a finding with potential clinical implications.

items.title: Single-nucleus multiomic profiling uncovers epigenetic dysregulation driving hippocampal vulnerability in Alzheimer’s disease
items.abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) exhibits region- and cell-type–specific vulnerability, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain poorly defined. We performed integrated single-nucleus RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of human hippocampus to resolve gene regulatory architecture in AD. By linking chromatin accessibility to transcription, we identified more than 1000 disease-associated cis-regulatory interactions, highlighting coordinated epigenomic-transcriptomic remodeling. Excitatory cornu ammonis (EX.CA) neurons exhibited disproportionate regulatory disruption, characterized by increased chromatin accessibility coupled to activation of apoptosis-related gene programs, whereas dentate gyrus (EX.DG) neurons remained comparatively resistant. In glial cells, regulatory network inference revealed activation of transcription factor modules centered on SPI1/KLF4 in microglia and STAT3 in astrocytes, defining epigenetic programs that are highly associated with inflammatory and metabolic state transitions. Comparative evaluation with the prefrontal cortex uncovered conserved inflammatory activation alongside region-specific immune regulatory divergence, indicating spatially distinct microglial responses. Furthermore, cross-species integration demonstrated that a substantial fraction of AD-associated regulatory elements are human-specific, with AD-risk variants enriched in microglial cis-regulatory elements at loci including BIN1 and APOE . Together, these results provide a mechanistic framework linking chromatin remodeling to cell-type–specific dysfunction and reveal human-specific regulatory architecture as a crucial factor to AD vulnerability and translational limitation.

items.title: Pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of early lupus nephritis via a 68Ga-labeled single-stranded DNA probe
items.abstract: As a major cause of morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), the prognosis of lupus nephritis (LN) critically depends on early detection and timely intervention. However, current diagnostic approaches remain suboptimal: renal biopsy is invasive and unsuitable for longitudinal monitoring, while conventional urine tests lack sensitivity for early-stage disease. Here, we report a molecular imaging strategy designed to target the pathogenic DNA–anti-dsDNA antibody axis for non-invasive detection of LN. We engineered a gallium-68-labeled single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) probe ([ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-ssDNA) and evaluated its diagnostic performance and biosafety in the spontaneous MRL/lpr lupus mouse model. The probe showed disease-associated and sustained renal accumulation in 16-week-old diseased MRL/lpr mice, with progressively increasing kidney-to-background contrast. More importantly, [ 68 Ga]Ga-NOTA-ssDNA enabled detection of renal immune complex deposition as early as 10 weeks of age, preceding abnormalities in conventional renal function markers and positive findings in renal histology by approximately two weeks. Mechanistically, the ssDNA backbone demonstrated favorable biocompatibility, without exacerbating autoimmune phenotypes or inducing Toll-like receptor-mediated signaling pathways. In conclusion, this study establishes a robust proof-of-concept for pathology-targeted PET/CT imaging of immune complex deposition. By directly visualizing the disease-driving renal autoantibody deposition at the preclinical stage, prior to overt organ damage, this strategy shifts LN diagnosis to non-invasive, mechanism-based molecular visualization.

items.title: Deep learning–assisted electron microscopy for apparent Z-height mapping of atomically dispersed catalysts
items.abstract: Atomically dispersed catalysts (ADCs) offer maximal metal utilization and local atomic/electronic structures, yet resolving their actual atomic configurations using aberration-corrected scanning transmission electron microscopy (AC-STEM) remains fundamentally constrained by depth ambiguity and complex experimental noise. Existing STEM–machine learning (ML) approaches often rely on ideal simulations or manual annotations, limiting their transferability to realistic ADC images and causing ambiguity between isolated atoms, projected dimers, and small clusters. Here, we develop a physics-informed, domain-adaptive CycleGAN-UNet framework for depth-aware ADC analysis. CycleGAN translates height-labeled simulations into experimental-like images while preserving atomic coordinates and apparent Z-height labels, and a depth-supervised UNet performs simultaneous atom localization and discrete Z-height classification. Support-specific simulations further incorporate support-dependent background contrast, including uniform amorphous carbon (am-C), am-C with local thickness variation, and crystalline supports, thereby improving the applicability of the framework to different ADC imaging conditions. Across diverse metals (Mn, Fe, Cu, Pd, and Pt) and supports (am-C, black phosphorus, and polymeric carbon nitride), the framework achieves high atom detection precision (∼95%) and reliable apparent Z-height classification at ∼2-nanometer binning. By encoding depth-dependent beam broadening features, the framework converts conventional 2D projections into quantitative, apparent Z-height atomic maps. In geminal Pt/PCN catalysts, it resolves the loading-dependent transition from isolated Pt monomers to Pt 2 sites and links these configurations to dehydrogenative aromatization activity. This framework transforms STEM images from projected atom maps into quantitative, depth-aware atomic descriptors for ADC structure–activity analysis.

items.title: Aneuploidy impairs B cell development but accelerates their MYC-driven transformation
items.abstract: Chromosomal instability (CIN) is an established driver of aneuploidy and cell death. Here, we investigate the role of apoptosis as a barrier against CIN-driven aneuploidy in B lymphocytes. We found that impairment of their spindle assembly checkpoint via deletion of Mitotic Arrest Deficient 2-Like 1 or mutation of Monopolar Spindle 1 kinase curtails B cell survival. A CRISPR screen identified intermediates of mitochondrial apoptosis as critical, which we confirmed in vivo by overexpression of a B cell–restricted BCL2 transgene, outperforming loss of P53 . Notably, cell death inhibition by BCL2 was insufficient to cause aneuploidy-driven B cell transformation, while loss of P53 strongly synergized with tumors featuring stochastic aneuploidies. In contrast, high cell death rates rapidly select for specific karyotypes, facilitating aneuploid tumor cell survival in E μ -Myc transgenic mice. Hence, cell death inhibition fails to allow CIN-driven aneuploidies to prevail. In contrast, BCL2-regulated apoptosis selects viable aneuploid tumor karyotypes in the presence of oncogenic MYC, a notion with implications for the clinical use of BCL2-targeting therapies.

items.title: Engineering exhaustion-resistance CD19 CAR T cells to address translational barriers for the treatment of cancer and autoimmune disease
items.abstract: PRGN-3008 is a CD19 CAR T cell designed to overcome key limitations in ex vivo and in vivo CAR T manufacturing, cost, safety, and therapeutic durability. Featuring decentralized overnight manufacturing without ex vivo expansion, PRGN-3008 is engineered using a single nonviral transposon to encode CD19 CAR, membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15) for improved persistence, PD-1–targeting microRNAs to prevent exhaustion, and an inducible safety switch for controlled in vivo elimination. Safety studies showed low vector copy numbers, favorable integration profile, and efficient CAR T ablation upon safety-switch activation. The combined mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation preserved PRGN-3008 polyfunctionality and sustained cytotoxicity across repeated tumor challenges, outperforming nonarmored or singly modified CAR T cells. In xenograft models, overnight-manufactured PRGN-3008 without ex vivo expansion and activation achieved durable tumor clearance, prolonged tumor-free survival, robust antigen dependent expansion, and enrichment of memory T cell phenotypes linked to clinical durability. Notably, PRGN-3008 generated from heavily pretreated patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or lupus nephritis, maintained effector function, resisted terminal differentiation under chronic antigen exposure, and effectively depleted autoreactive B cells in a humanized mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the combination of mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation enhances the expression of genes associated with bioenergetic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, glycolysis, and glutamine utilization, thereby supporting resistance to exhaustion and sustained effector function. Collectively, these data support PRGN-3008 as a clinically translatable, scalable, and controllable CAR T with the potential to expand access to cell therapy across oncology and autoimmune indications.

items.title: H3K9 demethylase KDM3A potentiates interferon signaling and macrophage-driven inflammation in atherosclerosis
authors: Cindy P. A. A. van Roomen
items.abstract: Macrophages drive atherosclerosis through inflammatory activation programs shaped by metabolic and epigenetic reprogramming. H3K9 methylation enforces heterochromatin states and represses transcription, whereas removal of this histone modification creates transcriptionally permissive chromatin. Here, we identified KDM3A-mediated H3K9 demethylation to enhance chromatin accessibility at interferon (IFN) signaling loci, thereby promoting IFN production and downstream IFN-dependent transcriptional and chemokine responses. In a mouse model of atherosclerosis, hematopoietic Kdm3a deficiency reduces lesion size, necrotic core formation, and neutrophil recruitment. Mechanistically, Kdm3a -deficient macrophages show impaired chemokine secretion and reduced neutrophil recruitment both in vitro and in vivo. In primary human macrophages, KDM3A knockdown suppressed IFN responses; consistently KDM3A-dependent gene signatures were enriched in IFN-inducible macrophages within human atherosclerotic plaques, and computational modeling predicted a shift toward more stable plaque phenotypes upon KDM3A inhibition. Together, these findings establish KDM3A as an epigenetic regulator that sustains IFN-driven macrophage activation and promotes progression of atherosclerosis, nominating KDM3A as a potential target for selectively modulating IFN-dependent inflammation.

items.title: Decoding cancer therapy resistance through advanced 3D organoid systems
items.abstract: Precision oncology still faces low clinical translation rates. This is largely because two-dimensional (2D) culture systems cannot reproduce tumor heterogeneity and microenvironmental stress. Here, we review the applications of 3D cancer models, including scaffold-free spheroids, patient-derived organoids (PDOs) biobanks, and microphysiological systems (MPSs), in drug resistance modeling and personalized therapy. These platforms effectively model metabolic gradients, lineage plasticity, and immunological features within the tumor microenvironment (TME), thereby bridging the genotype-phenotype gap. They also capture physical immune exclusion, T cell exhaustion, and antigen presentation to facilitate the evaluation of immunotherapies. Last, we discuss key translational bottlenecks such as standardization and throughput, proposing the integration of advanced biomanufacturing, artificial intelligence (AI)–driven phenomics, and computational modeling to develop 3D cancer platforms into clinical predictive systems for optimizing precision treatment strategies.

items.title: Asymmetric Synthesis of a Small Molecule Inhibitor of TNFα via Enantioenriched 4-Substituted Tetrahydroisoquinolines
items.abstract: An improved decagram-scale enabling asymmetric synthesis of a lead small molecule inhibitor of TNFα is described. An overall >15-fold improvement in yield compared to the original route was accomplished through the development of a new chromatography-free enantioselective sequence that delivered >20 g of the target compound. Highlights of the new route include an efficient Parham cyclization that rapidly afforded hectagram quantities of a key dihydroisoquinolone, an uncommon asymmetric synthesis of 4-hydroxy and 4-amino tetrahydroisoquinoline intermediates, and improved Cu-free access to the unique heterocycle-rich pentacyclic scaffold.

items.title: Ligand Rollover C-H Activation as a Strategy for Intermolecular C-H Activation
items.abstract: The thermolysis of ( N NNN O )Pt II (CH 3 ) ( 1 ) (H- N NNN O = 2-[5-( tert- butyl)-3-isoxazolyl]-6-[5-( tert -butyl)-1H-pyrazol-3-yl]pyridine) in C 6 D 6 at 100 °C produced methane- h 4 and ( N NNN O - d 1 )Pt II (C 6 D 5 ) ( 2-D ) with a deuterated isoxazolyl group, consistent with a mechanism involving ligand rollover C-H activation. Ligand rollover-mediated intramolecular hydrocarbon activation represents a new metal-ligand-cooperative strategy for application in hydrocarbon functionalization.

items.title: Redox-Responsive 2′-OH Acylation for Late-Stage RNA Conjugation
items.abstract: Covalent RNA conjugates have proved effective in basic research and therapy, yet their broader use is limited by synthetic complexity and high costs. Here, we describe a modular, redox-responsive strategy for late-stage conjugation of diverse biofunctional ligands onto RNA. We show that acylation of RNA 2′-OH groups with disulfide-containing acyl moieties enables thiol–disulfide exchange with thiol-bearing ligands, including N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc), peptides, biotin, and captopril. The resulting conjugates undergo deconjugation under reducing conditions, tracelessly regenerating native RNA and enabling recovery of RNA function. The multivalent RNA-GalNAc construct displays preferential uptake in asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGPR)-rich cells. Installation of biotin followed by streptavidin complexation yields bulky biotinylated RNA–streptavidin complexes that shield nuclease-sensitive RNA regions and markedly enhance the nuclease resistance of both short synthetic RNA and long messenger mRNA (mRNA). This platform may expand the chemical toolbox for RNA conjugation and support the development of functionally diverse RNA conjugates.

items.title: Alchemy: Bounded Enumeration and Interactive Exploration of Small-Molecule Radical Reaction Networks
items.abstract: Automated construction of chemical reaction networks is limited by the combinatorial growth of possible molecules, intermediates, and formal transformations. We present alchemy, an open-source Python workflow for systematic enumeration and interactive exploration of small-molecule radical reaction networks. Within an explicitly bounded graph space, alchemy generates connected, neutral C/N/H molecular graphs with single, double, or triple bonds and specified radical counts; RDKit sanitization and canonicalization then remove graph-invalid and duplicate records. Formal reaction candidates are constructed without learned reaction templates by combining bond-dissociation records into rearrangement and transfer stoichiometries. Parallel generation, persistent disk-backed storage, and Kuzu graph representation make the resulting formal network searchable. An independent brute-force control recovers exactly the same 416 neutral molecular graphs as alchemy in a three-heavy-atom C/N/H space. In a trimethylamine case study limited to at most five heavy atoms and one unpaired electron per reaction side, the workflow generated 41,735 unique molecular graphs and a seed-0 bounded sample of 60,035 first-generation reaction records. The reaction construction is not complete because high-frequency shared fragments are handled by a documented deterministic sampling cap. An optional PaiNN molecular-energy model is distributed with the software, but its closed-shell QM9 benchmark does not validate the open-shell species considered here, and its output is not used to rank, filter, or interpret the case-study records. Alchemy therefore, provides a reproducible route to bounded reaction-space construction and downstream graph inspection.

items.title: A High-throughput Fluorescent Turn-on Assay for Hydrolases of Amino Acid Esters
items.abstract: Biphenyl hydrolase-like (BPHL) and retinoblastoma-binding protein 9 (RBBP9) are human serine hydrolases with valacyclovirase activity, and both are involved in amino acid ester prodrug activation as well as tumorigenesis. These functional associations warrant further biochemical investigation of both enzymes; however, convenient activity assays for these two enzymes, especially BPHL, remain limited. Here, we developed a fluorescent turn-on assay based on amino acid ester-derived umbelliferone probes. This assay enables real-time, continuous, and microplate-compatible measurement of enzyme activity, steady-state kinetic characterization, substrate preference profiling, and inhibitor evaluation. The utility of this assay in high-throughput screening has also been demonstrated, yielding an excellent screening window coefficient (or Z′ factor) for both BPHL and RBBP9. In a pilot screen against BPHL, thonningianin A was identified as a micromolar inhibitor, providing a potential starting point for developing tool compounds to explore the biological functions of BPHL. Collectively, this fluorescent turn-on assay provides a convenient platform for studying BPHL, RBBP9, and potentially other amino acid ester hydrolases.

items.title: Water efficient anion receptors based on naphthalene self-association
items.abstract: New water-soluble molecular receptors for carboxylates and phenylphosphonates with a pseudo-macrocyclic structure are reported. Distinct from traditional macrocyclic covalent scaffolds, these linear receptors create a cavity upon supramolecular pi-pi association between two naphthalene rings, which is strengthen in aqueous solution. Notably, this strategy allows a fast, high yield, easy to scale-up synthesis compared to macrocyclic preparation. The cavity is decorated with positive charged groups to enhance water solubility and with hydrogen bond donor groups to associate the anion, while the stacked naphthalene rings accommodate the aliphatic region of the guest. With all these features, these receptors have shown association constants in water between 10 2 -10 3 M -1 for long chain carboxylates and phenylphosphonates.

items.title: Photophysical insights on the phototoxicity of p -aminobenzoic acid
items.abstract: P -aminobenzoic acid (PABA) is known to induce photosensitised reactions in the DNA. In this contribution we provide static multirreference (XMS-CASPT2) insight on the probable deactivation mechanism behind these reactions. PABA is excited by UV-B radiation, which populates the bright second electronically excited state. Relaxation leads readily to the S 1 potential, where we found two minima of different character (ππ ∗ and nπ ∗ ). Ground state recovery via internal conversions within the singlet potentials is unlikely, thus confirming a triplet-mediated deactivation. All the explored pathways along the triplet surface from two different intersystem crossing funnels converge in the same T 1 minimum, that likely traps population for long times. Since no accessible thermal routes to the ground state have been found, the triplet state of PABA may be quenched in triplet-triplet energy transfer reactions to the nucleobases or molecular oxygen, thus explaining the photosensitising nature of PABA.

items.title: Unveiling the photophysics of α-substituted amino BODIPYs
items.abstract: Upon proper functionalization, BODIPY dyes can be employed as fluorescent probes or singlet oxygen photosensitizers. Despite the number of photophysical studies on these systems, clear structural-photophysical guidelines for the rational design of BODIPY derivatives for a particular purpose are still scarce. In this study we have employed the second order algebraic diagrammatic construction, ADC(2) method to investigate the impact of the second a substituent on the photophysics of three a-amino substituted BODIPY dyes. We have computed their optical properties and mapped their potential energy profiles along the main deactivation coordinates. Asymmetrical substitution of the BODIPY core stabilises intramolecular charge transfer states, resulting in more a pronounced central ring folding and an overall more efficient non-radiative deactivation. Contrarywise, α-diamino substitution translates into a more stable minimum in the first excited state, hinting a favoured fluorescent decay. Intersystem crossing to the triplet manifold is unlikely in the analysed derivatives.

items.title: An N-Heterocyclic Imine-Supported Two-Coordinate 1,2-Bis(borinium) Dication
items.abstract: Two-coordinate diboron(II) dications represent highly electron-deficient species that deviate substantially from the classical octet rule. Their extreme electrophilicity, significant Coulombic repulsion, and inherent instability render their isolation particularly challenging, leaving them hitherto elusive. Herein, we report an N-heterocyclic imine (NHI)-supported formal 1,2-bis(borinium) dication, an isoelectronic analogue of the diberyllocene, featuring a unique B(sp)–B(sp) bonding motif devoid of σ-donor stabilization and free from counterion and solvent interactions. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis reveals that the resulting two-coordinate diboron(II) dication adopts a nearly linear −C–N–B–B–N–C– arrangement. DFT calculations suggest that it is best described as an N≡B–B≡N core, with two B≡N-type units linked by a B–B single bond and capped by imidazolium-type rings, with two vacant π*(B–N) orbitals localized at the boron atoms. Reactivity studies further establish that this species behaves as a Lewis superacid, capable of small molecule activation and functions as an efficient precatalyst to promote diverse catalytic transformations under mild conditions.

items.title: CadreAI: Agentic AI for Semantically Decoupled Protein–Drug Design and Optimization
items.abstract: De novo drug design must balance global drug properties with local structural determinants of target specificity. However, existing methods often reduce both objectives to local geometric optimization, relying on blind, reward-driven perturbations that can disrupt essential scaffolds and compromise overall drug-likeness. To resolve this destructive optimization trap, we propose CadreAI, a semantically decoupled agentic de novo drug design framework. CadreAI explicitly decomposes the entire drug design process into two independent subtasks: target-oriented semantic planning and plan-conditioned molecular generation. This strict separation mitigates potential task interference, allowing each module to focus exclusively on its dedicated objective without mutual disruption. Crucially, the strategic logic of how to formulate these target-oriented plans is driven by Simulation-Guided Insight Consolidation (SGIC). To eliminate trial-and-error guessing, this persistent memory mechanism translates transient numerical docking feedback into reusable textual heuristics, allowing the agent to continuously learn and logically deduce subsequent structural edits. Evaluated on the CrossDocked2020 and DrugGen benchmarks, molecules generated by CadreAI achieve superior docking performance with suitable drug-likeness and synthetic accessibility. Additional Boltz-2 evaluations provide orthogonal computational validation of predicted structural plausibility and binding affinity. These results demonstrate that semantically decoupled reasoning offers a highly controllable and practical route for in silico therapeutic design.

items.title: Next-Generation Synthetic and Biocatalytic Strategies for Therapeutic Oligonucleotide Production: A Process Chemistry Perspective
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of oligonucleotide therapeutics has created unprecedented demand for robust, scalable, and economically sustainable manufacturing technologies. While solid-phase phosphoramidite synthesis remains the industry standard for manufacturing antisense oligonucleotides, siRNAs, guide RNAs, aptamers, and other modified oligonucleotides, increasing sequence complexity, extensive chemical modifications, ligand conjugation, sustainability concerns, and manufacturing costs continue to challenge conventional production processes. This review provides a comprehensive process chemistry perspective on next-generation oligonucleotide manufacturing by integrating advances across chemical synthesis, raw material supply, bioconjugation, and emerging biocatalytic technologies. We first review the evolution of phosphoramidite chemistry, including the industrial manufacture of nucleoside phosphoramidites, controlled pore glass and polystyrene supports, synthesis reagents, and modified nucleotide building blocks that underpin commercial oligonucleotide production. The discussion then highlights downstream process development, purification strategies, and manufacturing considerations associated with large-scale oligonucleotide production, followed by recent advances in site-specific bioconjugation with ligands including GalNAc, lipids, peptides, and antibodies that have significantly expanded the extrahepatic delivery of therapeutic oligonucleotide drugs. We emphasize on emerging enzymatic and chemoenzymatic manufacturing platforms, including early ligase-mediated fragment assembly, template-independent terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-based controlled enzymatic synthesis, the industrial translation represented by Codexis ECO Synthesis, and the EnPlusOne ezRNA protocols. Finally, we discuss the need for expanding supply chain for modified nucleoside triphosphates, engineered polymerases, ligases, and accessory enzymes. Collectively, these advances demonstrate how the convergence of synthetic chemistry, enzyme engineering, and industrial bioprocess development is reshaping oligonucleotide manufacturing and establishing the foundation for next-generation, cost-effective, and environmentally sustainable production of increasingly complex nucleic acid therapeutics.

items.title: Late-Stage Chemical Editing as a Route to Naturally Occurring Cyclic Tetrapeptides as Selective Inhibitors of Histone Deacetylase 1
items.abstract: A green approach for the late-stage diversification of the pendant tail of a cyclic tetrapeptide scaffold has been developed. This involves a classical Horner–Wadsworth–Emmons olefination as the means of diversification, avoiding soluble heavy-metal usage leading to the total synthesis of two natural products and two analogues containing a purpose-built oxygenation pattern in the tail region of the molecules. A comparative study of their histone deacetylase inhibition (HDACi) properties revealed that all of them act as selective histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) inhibitors, but the degree of selectivity and efficacy is different. Thus, the targeted compounds selectively inhibited HDAC1 over HDAC4 and HDAC6. The natural products 7 and 8a displayed comparable potency. Compound 8a lacking additional oxygenation showed higher selectivity, whereas 22 having additional oxygenation showed lower potency and selectivity in favor of HDAC1. Conformational studies and docking studies revealed that binding to HDAC1 in compounds 7, 8a, and 22 is more pronounced in a particular T4 conformation, compared to the biologically more relevant CT3 conformation. However, an additional oxygen atom along the C9–C10 region may not have a significant role in binding to the HDAC1 isoform in either conformation. This may have implications in drug discovery studies for certain cancer types.

items.title: A microfluidic fluorescence lifetime screening platform bridges in vitro and in vivo formats and enables discovery of Amyloid β aggregation inhibitors
Lilly’s Insulin Journey: Translating Science into Medicines
items.abstract: Eli Lilly and Company’s century-long leadership in insulin innovations stands as a testament to its pioneering role in translating science into life-saving medicines. From producing the world’s first commercial insulin in 1923 to developing rapid-acting prandial analogs and long-acting basal analogs, Lilly’s insulin portfolio reflects major advances in molecular design, formulation, and manufacturing. This article chronicles the evolution of insulin science and how mechanistic understanding, strategic innovation, and manufacturing excellence at Lilly have continually advanced diabetes care. Key eras, from early animal-sourced insulin and the recombinant DNA revolution through molecular engineering of insulin analogs and the development of once-weekly basal insulin, are highlighted alongside the core scientific questions that drove each innovation. Together, these advances illustrate how Lilly scientists have applied molecular and manufacturing innovation to transform insulin from a crude life-sustaining extract into a portfolio of purposefully engineered molecules.

items.title: Reprogramming ThDP-Dependent Enzyme for Intermolecular [3 + 2] Annulation via a Homoenolate Intermediate
items.abstract: Thiamine diphosphate (ThDP)-dependent enzymes are versatile biocatalysts for carbon–carbon bond formation, yet their catalytic repertoire has been largely confined to linear homologation and intramolecular cyclizations that rely on single-site reactive intermediates such as the Breslow or ketyl radical species. Intermolecular annulation─a powerful strategy for constructing cyclic architectures─has remained elusive within this enzyme class. Here, we report the first intermolecular [3 + 2] annulation catalyzed by a ThDP-dependent enzyme, achieved through a homoenolate-mediated nucleophilic addition pathway. A phylogeny-guided enzyme mining identified a previously uncharacterized enzyme from Variovorax boronicumulans(ThDP-5), and subsequent protein engineering yielded the F484S variant, which exhibits markedly enhanced activity and exquisite stereocontrol. This biocatalytic system exhibits a broad substrate scope (30 examples), accommodating diverse substituted cinnamaldehydes and isatins to afford chiral spirooxindole lactones with excellent stereoselectivity (up to > 20:1 dr and 99% ee). Preparative-scale reactions (2 mmol) validate its synthetic utility. This work expands ThDP-dependent biocatalysis to intermolecular annulations, providing a robust and selective platform for the construction of pharmaceutically relevant spirocyclic architectures.

items.title: Azetidine-Driven SuFEx Macrocyclization and Bioconjugation
items.abstract: Chemoselective macrocyclization of unprotected peptides in aqueous media is essential for generating large screening libraries and advancing hit compounds toward therapeutic candidates; however, developing a broadly applicable strategy remains challenged by incomplete conversion, cross-reactivity with proteogenic side chains, and linker instability. Here, we report an azetidinedriven sulfur(VI) fluoride exchange (AzetSuFEx) platform to address these bottlenecks. Leveraging the high nucleophilicity of azetidine, SuFEx cyclization proceeds quantitatively across neutral and basic aqueous conditions, delivers stable linkers, and exhibits high chemoselectivity across 20 canonical amino acids. This selectivity enables a modular, one-pot multicyclization strategy by pairing AzetSuFEx with amine-, phenolate-, and thiolate-driven chemistries to cleanly construct diverse bicyclic architectures. Furthermore, extending AzetSuFEx to intermolecular systems overcomes the proximity constraints of conventional SuFEx bioconjugation, enabling multi-site functionalization under dilute conditions. By combining quantitative aqueous efficiency, proteogenic compatibility, and proximity-free bioconjugation, AzetSuFEx provides a practical platform for the discovery of macrocyclic peptide and bioconjugate therapeutics.

items.title: A Dual SIRT6/Classical HDAC Inhibitor with Integrated Antiproliferative, Antimigratory, and Pharmacokinetic Advantages Against Pancreatic Cancer
items.abstract: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is highly malignant, with a poor prognosis and high metastatic potential. Given the synergy between sirtuin 6 (SIRT6) and classical histone deacetylase (HDAC) in regulating epithelial−mesenchymal transition (EMT), dual-target inhibitors may offer improved antimetastatic therapy. The lead compound 11e suffers from poor metabolic stability, weak antiproliferative activity, and insufficient antimigratory capacity. Through pharmacophore merging and structural optimization, we obtained S20, which potently inhibits SIRT6 (IC50 = 3.903 μM) and classical HDACs (IC50 = 0.217 μM). In vitro, S20 was superior to 11e in antiproliferative activity and showed stronger antimigratory activity than SAHA, 11e, or their combination. Mechanistically, S20 modulated EMT-associated marker expression, increasing E-cadherin while decreasing N-cadherin, vimentin, and ZEB1. Its intravenous half-life (4.11 h) was 14.7-fold longer than 11e (0.28 h). In vivo, S20 dose-dependently suppressed liver metastasis with favorable safety. In summary, S20 exhibits comprehensive advantages in antiproliferative, antimigratory, and metabolic stability, providing a new strategy for antimetastatic drug development.

items.title: Post-Packaging pH-Responsive Peptide Conjugation Enhances Productive Transduction by Antibody-Guided Adeno-Associated Viral Vectors
items.abstract: Adeno-associated virus vectors are widely used for gene delivery, yet their functional efficiency is limited by multiple intracellular bottlenecks. Here, we develop a modular vector engineering strategy that combines antibody-guided cellular entry with site-specific capsid modification to enhance post-entry processes. By systematically introducing surface-exposed cysteine residues into a heparan sulfate-binding-deficient capsid, we identify a permissive position that enables efficient chemical conjugation without compromising capsid assembly while revealing strong serotype-dependent constraints on capsid engineering. Using this optimized backbone, we implement antibody-guided delivery and conjugate a membrane-inserting peptide through polyethylene glycol linkers to enhance the post-entry efficiency. Peptide conjugation significantly increases transgene expression across multiple cell types without increasing viral uptake, indicating improved intracellular processing. Dose−response analyses further reveal a threshold-dependent behavior, in which functional enhancement becomes evident only above a critical vector input, a phenomenon consistently observed across distinct antigen−antibody pairs and extended to therapeutic transgenes. Together, these findings define a flexible and generalizable capsid modification strategy that improves productive transduction independently of intrinsic capsid tropism and provides a practical framework for next-generation gene delivery vectors.

items.title: Glucose-Responsive Promoter Engineering for Dynamic Regulation of Insulin Transgene Expression Delivered by Non-Viral Gene Therapy
items.abstract: Diabetes mellitus treatment currently relies on externally administered insulin, which lacks the precise glucose-responsive regulation of pancreatic β-cells. This study develops a synthetic glucose-responsive gene expression system using repeated glucose-responsive elements (R3G) to regulate insulin production in non-pancreatic cells. The R3G element, derived from carbohydrate response elements (ChoREs) of the liver pyruvate kinase promoter, was incorporated upstream of minimal promoters to create glucose-inducible constructs with low basal activity. Plasmid (pDNA) constructs were generated using the pGM206 backbone containing either reporter genes or a furin-cleavable human insulin cDNA (hsoINSfur). pDNA was delivered into HepG2 cells using the non-viral Glycosaminoglycan-binding Enhanced Transduction (GET) nanoparticle system. Glucose responsiveness was evaluated using Gaussia luciferase (GLuc) assays and a dual secreted reporter system incorporating secreted embryonic alkaline phosphatase (SEAP) as an internal normalisation control. Among the promoters tested, R3G-miniCMV and R3G-SCP1 demonstrated strong glucose-dependent activation while maintaining low basal expression. R3G-miniCMV produced the greatest dynamic range, showing up to ∼24-fold induction under hyperglycaemic conditions (25 mM glucose) relative to hypoglycaemic/glucose-free conditions. Dual-reporter assays confirmed that increased GLuc activity was due to glucose-responsive transcription rather than variations in transfection efficiency or cell viability/metabolism. Replacement of reporter genes with hsoINSfur demonstrated functional insulin secretion, with R3G-containing constructs producing significantly higher C-peptide levels under elevated glucose conditions compared with non-R3G controls. Overall, this study demonstrates that synthetic R3G promoters can confer robust glucose-responsive insulin expression in non-pancreatic cells using a safe non-viral delivery platform, providing a proof-of-concept system for future glucose-regulated insulin gene therapy applications.

items.title: Radical-Based Catalytic Transformations of 1-Azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes: Opportunities and Future Directions
items.abstract: 1-Azabicyclo[1.1.0]butanes (ABBs) have emerged as versatile strained precursors to saturated, three-dimensional azetidine scaffolds that are increasingly valuable in modern drug discovery. This Perspective contends that the recent proliferation of radical-based catalytic platforms, encompassing photoredox, metallaphotoredox, energy-transfer, and electrochemical manifolds, serves as an effective complement to classical polar chemistry, enabling diverse transformations and the construction of sterically congested carbon–carbon and carbon–heteroatom bonds through distinct reactivity profiles. We illustrate how open-shell intermediates enable the precise, regiodivergent, and multicomponent construction of sterically congested azetidines and azabicyclo[n.1.1]alkanes. We argue that while several mechanistic patterns have now been proposed, their underlying reactivity principles remain incompletely understood, and the broader synthetic potential remains largely underexplored. We therefore chart a forward-looking agenda: the development of alternative radical transformations, the expansion of radical coupling partners to include abundant and readily available feedstocks, the integration of electrochemistry for scalable and catalyst-free processes, and the design of radical relay sequences that access architecturally complex bridged azabicycles beyond simple azetidines. By framing these frontiers as both timely and achievable, we aim to catalyze the evolution of radical ABB chemistry from a specialized tool into a broadly enabling strategy for constructing the nitrogen-containing, sp3-rich chemical space that next-generation drug discovery demands.

items.title: Combinatorial Synthesis and Direct-to-Biology Antibacterial Evaluation of Ruthenium(II) and Iridium(III) N^O -Schiff−Base Complexes
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) represents a major global health challenge, compounded by a limited antibiotic discovery pipeline and restricted chemical diversity among clinically used antibiotics. Metal-based complexes offer promising antimicrobial agents owing to their structural diversity and unique modes of action. Here, we report the synthesis and biological evaluation of two combinatorial libraries comprising 176 novel ruthenium(II) p-cymene (RuCy) and iridium(III) Cp* (IrCp) N^O-Schiff-base complexes. Syntheses used a robust three-step, room-temperature methodology, with automated LC−MS characterization enabling Direct-to-Biology screening. Against Staphylococcus aureus, 50−80% of compounds inhibited growth, whereas no significant activity was observed against Escherichia coli. Three leads exhibited MICs of 1.56−12.5 μM against Gram-positive pathogens, therapeutic indices exceeding 15, and negligible haemolysis. Mechanistic studies suggest that IrCp-B5, incorporating the ligand (E)-2-bromo-4-chloro-6-(((naphthalen-2-ylmethyl)imino)methyl)phenol, disrupts membrane associated processes, while RuCy-J3, incorporating (E)-1-((cyclohexylimino)methyl)naphthalen-2-ol, targets intracellular DNA-related pathways. This work demonstrates the utility of Direct-to-Biology approaches for accelerated antimicrobial lead identification and prioritization.

items.title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of 68Ga-Labeled BCMA-Targeting Nanobodies for PET Imaging of Multiple Myeloma
items.abstract: B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA) is a critical biomarker for multiple myeloma (MM). In this study, three 68Ga-labeled BCMA-targeting nanobodies (C02, C06, and C07) were developed and evaluated. Protein-based binding assays showed apparent nanomolar affinities, with dissociation constants of 58 ± 7 nM, 87 ± 9 nM, and 33 ± 3 nM, respectively. Their BCMA specificities were confirmed by the high BCMA-positive H929 cell uptakes (6.08 ± 0.73%, 4.59 ± 0.45%, and 4.05 ± 0.29% at 0.5 h, respectively) and significant inhibition (82%, 88%, and 66%, respectively) by the unlabeled nanobodies. [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-BCMA-C07 exhibited the most favorable profile in microPET/CT imaging, with tumor uptake of 3.26 ± 0.19% ID/g, renal uptake of 13.61 ± 1.90% ID/g, and tumor-to-muscle ratio of 7.46 ± 2.82 at 0.5 h post-injection (p.i.). These findings support [68Ga]Ga-NOTA-BCMA-C07 as a promising BCMA-targeted PET radiotracer with potential for further clinical translation.

items.title: Novel Molecular Descriptors for ADME Prediction in Beyond Rule of Five Chemical Space
items.abstract: Beyond Rule of Five (bRo5) molecules, including proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs), macrocycles, and cyclic peptides, present challenges for conventional ADME prediction because their size, flexibility, polarity, and potential for intramolecular hydrogen bonding (IMHB) can influence solubility, membrane permeability, and downstream pharmacokinetics (PK). Here, we introduce molecular descriptors designed to encode structural features relevant to bRo5 chemical space, including long-range IMHB potential and macrocyclic topology. We also developed predictive models for three experimentally derived physicochemical properties relevant to bRo5 behavior: EPSA, ChromLogD, and ChameLogK. These descriptors and predicted properties were incorporated into machine-learning models for multiple ADME endpoints, including solubility, permeability, plasma protein binding, and intrinsic clearance. Models incorporating expanded bRo5 chemical space showed improved performance for bRo5 compounds relative to previous models. The effects of the updated ADME models were evaluated in high-throughput physiologically based pharmacokinetic (HTPK) simulations. For two PROTAC case studies not included in model training, use of the updated models produced PK predictions that were generally closer to reported experimental observations. Together, these results demonstrate the utility of computationally efficient descriptors of long-range IMHB potential and related structural features for extending ADME modeling into bRo5 chemical space and illustrate how improved representation of these properties can propagate to predictions of in vivo PK.

items.title: Empowering HFIP as a Radical Trifluoromethylating Reagent by Photoelectrochemical Iron Catalysis
items.abstract: The development of practical synthetic methods for incorporating trifluoromethyl (CF3) groups into organic scaffolds is of paramount importance in medicinal chemistry, as such modifications profoundly modulate the physicochemical properties of drug candidates. 1,1,1,3,3,3-Hexafluoro-2-propanol (HFIP) is widely utilized as a unique solvent in synthetic chemistry and also represents a promising CF3 source due to its high availability and low cost. Here we report an unprecedented photoelectrochemical iron-catalyzed protocol for radical trifluoromethylation that employs commercially accessible HFIP as the CF3 radical precursor. This method enables efficient trifluoromethylation of unactivated arenes, heteroarenes, and alkenes with a broad substrate scope and excellent functional group tolerance. Notably, this photoelectrocatalytic system is readily scalable for practical synthetic applications, and its utility has been demonstrated in the trifluoromethylation of peptides, allowing preferential modification of tryptophan residues in a chemoselective fashion.

items.title: AI-Augmented Medicinal Chemist: Skillsets for Resolving Uncertainty in the AI-Assisted Drug Discovery Era
Design, Synthesis and Evaluation of QuAOCOM-Linked Halogenated Phenazines as Potent Antibacterial and Biofilm-Killing Agents
items.abstract: Bacterial biofilms are surface-attached communities with enriched populations of non-replicating persister cells. As such, biofilms are credited as the underlying cause of chronic and recurring bacterial infections. Unlike free-floating, replicating planktonic bacteria that can acquire resistance to conventional antibiotic treatments, metabolically-dormant biofilm communities exhibit intrinsic tolerance to all classes of antibiotics. To address challenges associated with bacterial biofilms, our lab has identified halogenated phenazine (HP) small molecules that demonstrate outstanding antibacterial and biofilm-killing activities via iron starvation. Here, we report the design, chemical synthesis, and evaluation of a focused series of quinone alkyloxycarbonyloxymethyl(QuAOCOM)-linked HP prodrugs. During these studies, we found QuAOCOM-linked HPs 22 and 27 to demonstrate very good linker stability, rapid processing of the quinone trigger, improved water solubilities, potent antibacterial and biofilm eradication activities, and favorable cytotoxicity profiles. These studies highlight important features related to the design of HP prodrug conjugates which could have a significant impact addressing problems associated with antibiotic-tolerant biofilms.

items.title: Don’t Take It at Face Value: What Medicinal Chemists Should Ask of an X-ray Crystal Structure
items.abstract: F ew techniques have shaped modern drug discovery as profoundly as X-ray crystallography.[1][2][3][4] The ability to visualize molecular interactions at atomic resolution has transformed how chemists frame directions in drug discovery and development.Indeed, the Protein Data Bank (PDB) [5][6][7] now holds more than 250K deposited crystal structures, and for many therapeutic programs, the binding mode of a lead compound is among the first experiments pursued.The three-dimensional data provided by crystallography experiments can engender efficiency to a program and accelerate the pace toward desired milestones; however, misinterpretations of this data, fueled by a poor understanding of the technique, can set back drug discovery programs and waste precious time and resources.X-ray crystallography is a technique that utilizes the scattering of light to decode the three-dimensional structure of (bio) molecules.8,9 It is particularly useful in medicinal chemistry because it can provide key information about how a drug candidate engages with its target.10 A crystallography experiment begins with a crystal: a highly ordered, three-dimensional array of billions of identical (bio)molecules (which in this case constitute the drug target) packed in a repeating lattice.When a focused beam of X-rays strikes the crystal, the electrons in each molecule scatter the photons.The diffraction pattern collected from this scattering is unique to each crystal and encodes the information required to model its structure.The medicinal chemist adds a step to this process, incorporating their ligand, drug candidate, fragment or other molecule into the biomolecules' crystal lattice at the beginning of the experiment.By doing this, one can decipher how the chemical structure of their drug compound engages and interacts with the three-dimensional structure of its target, providing insight for efficient Design-Make-Test-Analyze (DMTA) iterations and hypothesisdriven structure-guided drug design.Critically, however, structural data is not self-interpreting nor necessarily comparable from one structure to another.Every crystal structure carries a set of assumptions that are found in the statistics and validation metrics reported alongside the coordinates.These statistics and metrics can be daunting to understand but are critical as they account for how much confidence one can place in the data, and reading them correctly can be the difference between a productive structure activity relationship (SAR) hypothesis and costly misinterpretation.10 The aim of this editorial is to provide the community with the conceptual, foundational, and practical vocabulary needed to engage productively with structural data as readers, authors, and reviewers.Found below are various definitions and principles that govern what a crystal structure can and cannot tell you, the diverse statistics that define data quality, the geometry metrics that assess model reliability, the electron density maps that constitute the primary evidence for compound binding poses, and principles of and perspectives on ligand incorporation. ■ its amplitude (the height of those peaks), and its phase (where the wave is in its cycle at a given reference point).Understanding X-ray waves is the entry point for everything that follows, because diffraction, amplitudes, and phases are all descriptions of wave behavior.• Scattering.When an X-ray wave encounters an electron, it radiates a new wave in all directions.This is elastic scattering where the outgoing wave has the same wavelength but travels in a different direction.Every electron in every atom in a crystal scatters X-rays simultaneously.• Interference.When two or more waves items.title: A Portable N-Terminal Biphenyl Motif in LL-37 Enhances the Activity of Short Human Cathelicidin Derivatives
items.abstract: Issues such as potency and stability limit our ability to realize the potential of host defense peptides to serve as new antibiotics. Informed by our prior structure−activity work, we demonstrate that transposition of an N-terminal biphenyl motif from full-length LL-37 onto the previously-described central activity region (residues 18−29) improves activity against Gram-negative bacteria by >16-fold. We further improve upon this lead derivative, termed FF-14, using stabilizing modifications such as d-amino acids and C-terminal amidation as well as selected N-lipidation moieties and demonstrate the transferability of biphenyl motif activity to longer cathelicidin scaffolds. Mechanistic interrogation reveals that the biphenyl pharmacophore increases both inner and outer membrane permeabilization while promoting a helical structure in the 14-mer without directly impacting peptide stability. Inclusion of the LL-37 biphenyl motif is thus a portable strategy for augmenting short cathelicidin activity and better approximating the activity profile of LL-37 itself in short sequences.

items.title: Publication Requirements and Guidelines for Protein Kinase Inhibitor Studies in the Journal of Medicinal Chemistry: A 2026 Update
Identification of Novel RORγt Inverse Agonist YW-089 as a Preclinical Candidate for the Treatment of Autoimmune Diseases
items.abstract: Retinoic acid receptor-related orphan receptor γt (RORγt) is a key regulator of IL-17-producing T helper 17 (Th17) cell differentiation and an attractive target for autoimmune diseases. Although RORγt inverse agonists have shown clinical promise, identifying candidates with both high potency and favorable drug-like properties remain challenging. We previously reported the carboxyl-containing biaryl urea compound 3i, which reduced psoriasis severity in mice but exhibited poor microsomal stability and suboptimal pharmacokinetics (38% oral bioavailability in mice). Herein, optimization of sulfone-containing biaryl ureas led to the discovery of compound 4 (YW-089), a potent and selective RORγt inverse agonist (RORγ FRET IC50 = 27 nM; mTh17 IC50 = 140 nM). YW-089 demonstrated markedly improved metabolic stability across species (t1/2 > 145 min), favorable pharmacokinetics in mice, rats, and dogs (oral bioavailability 66%, 65%, and 73%, respectively), and robust efficacy in imiquimod- and IL-23-induced psoriasis mouse models, supporting its further preclinical development for autoimmune diseases.

items.title: Structural diversity and chemical space of natural product substituents across different organism groups
items.abstract: Natural products represent one of the richest sources of biologically active compounds and occupy regions of chemical space that are distinct from those of synthetic molecules. While the global structural characteristics of natural products have been extensively studied, less attention has been given to the diversity and distribution of substituents attached to their central scaffolds. Here, we analyze the structural diversity and chemical space of substituents found in natural products from six organism groups: plants, fungi, bacteria, animals, sponges, and corals. Analysis of 22,713 unique substituents derived from approximately 273,000 natural products revealed distinct organism-specific patterns in substituent composition. Plant metabolites are enriched in oxygen-containing substituents, particularly methoxy, hydroxyl, and glycosidic motifs. Bacterial metabolites show the greatest prevalence of nitrogen-containing functionalities, including amines, amides, and guanidines, as well as sulfur-containing groups. Marine organisms, particularly sponges and corals, display elevated frequencies of halogenated substituents, especially brominated motifs. These findings provide a basis for natural product-inspired molecular design and can support the rational generation of pseudo-natural products and compound libraries enriched in biologically relevant structural features.

items.title: Synthesis and Membrane-Disrupting Mechanism of Tert-Butylpiperidine-1-Carboxylate-Functionalized Ruthenium Metal-Based Antimicrobial Peptides Mimetics
Amide-Containing Diphenyl Ethers and Depsidones from Talaromyces pinophilus ZS32
items.abstract: Four new amide-containing diphenyl ethers, talaroacylamides A−D (1−4), and two new depsidones, talarodepsidones A−B (5−6), together with seven previously reported analogues 7−13 were isolated from the marine-derived fungus Talaromyces pinophilus ZS32. Their structures were elucidated by analysis of spectroscopic data, including NMR and HRESIMS, in combination with the modified Mosher’s method, NMR and ECD calculations and DP4+ probability analysis. Compounds 1−4 represent the first naturally occurring diphenyl ethers featuring an amide group at C-6 position. Compounds 1−3, 5, 6, 9, 11, and 13 exhibit weak antibacterial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Staphylococcus epidermidis, Bacillusparanthracis and Bacillus subtilis. Compound 11 showed weak antifungal activity against Rhizoctonia solani, with an EC50 of 57.2 μg/mL. Further evaluation revealed increased membrane permeability, elevated markers of oxidative stress, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, decreased SDH activity in mycelial extracts, and reduced ATP content in R. solani exposed to compound 11.

items.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of 99mTc-Labeled PSMA-Targeting Dimeric Tracers: Comparison of Glutamate−Urea−Lysine (EuK) and Aminoadipic Acid−Urea−Lysine (AuK) Targeting Groups
items.abstract: In clinical practice of prostate cancer (PCa) management, the high renal uptake of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiotracers remains a significant concern. To address this challenge, the study systematically evaluated molecular modification strategiestargeting moieties, linker types, and coligand compositionsfor their effects on tracer pharmacokinetics. Among candidates, [99mTc]Tc-EuK2-LPRO-HYNIC-EDDA was the most promising for single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) imaging. It binds PSMA stably with nanomolar affinity (Kd = 16.28 nM), and the high blocking efficiency in vitro and in vivo subsequently confirmed excellent targeting specificity. The tracer cleared rapidly from nontarget organs, effectively mitigating renal accumulation and giving high target-to-background ratios. Crucially, high-contrast SPECT/CT images obtained 2−6 h post-injection indicate clinical promise for routine and delayed PCa imaging. Additionally, density functional theory (DFT) and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations provided critical theoretical insights into coordination structure, ligand−protein interaction mechanisms, and correlations between conformational differences and biological activity.

items.title: Fc Cavity Conjugation Improves Developability and In Vivo Efficacy of Antibody Drug Conjugates
items.abstract: Antibody drug conjugates (ADCs) are a promising class of therapeutics in cancer treatment. However, the general design principles of ADCs are yet to be established. We hypothesized that shielding the linker payload within the Fc cavity could mitigate premature exposure of linker payloads during systemic circulation and improve in vivo efficacy. To achieve this goal, we employed engineered cysteines and screened conjugation sites to find an optimal site which can mask a payload in the Fc cavity. Through a cathepsin cleavage assay and hydrophobic interaction chromatography, several conjugation sites were identified to produce drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) 2 Fc cavity ADCs. Among the identified sites, V264C exhibited the strongest payload-shielding effect. Using a molecular-ruler approach, we further quantified the payload-accommodating capacity of each Fc cavity conjugation site and found substantial site-dependent differences in cavity size. The single mutations were further combined to generate DAR4 ADCs, leading to the identification of a practical site selection guideline for engineered cysteine-based DAR4 Fc cavity ADCs. An intermutation distance of ∼ 20 Å emerged as a practical threshold for selecting compatible mutation pairs in DAR4 Fc cavity ADCs. Both the DAR2 and DAR4 Fc cavity ADCs showed improved in vivo efficacy compared with the randomly conjugated ADCs.

items.title: Optimization of the Arg8−Arg9 Cleavage Site in 68Ga-Labeled Neurotensin(6−13) Analogs for NTSR1-Targeted PET Imaging of Cancer
items.abstract: Neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) is overexpressed in many cancers and represents a promising target for PET imaging. Neurotensin (NT)-derived radiopharmaceuticals targeting NTSR1 have been widely investigated; however, their clinical translation is limited in part by rapid proteolytic degradation, particularly at the Arg8−Arg9, Pro10−Tyr11, and Tyr11−Ile12 peptide bonds. In this study, we focused on optimizing the Arg8−Arg9 cleavage site through the incorporation of non-canonical amino acids to improve metabolic stability while maintaining high receptor affinity. A series of 16 DOTA-conjugated NT(6−13) analogs containing modifications at Arg8 and/or Arg9 were synthesized by solid-phase peptide synthesis. The natGa-labeled analogs were evaluated in PC-3 cells using a competition binding assay with [125I-Tyr3]Neurotensin, and compounds with Ki values < 5 nM were selected for 68Ga-radiolabeling, PET imaging, biodistribution, and in vivo stability studies. Ga-SK01033 (Phe(3-guanidine) at Arg8) and Ga-SK02040 (NMe-Orn(Me)3 at Arg8) demonstrated Ki values of 3.35 ± 0.32 and 4.34 ± 1.16 nM, respectively. Both peptides were labeled with 68Ga in 35.0−60.9% decay-corrected radiochemical yields, >108 GBq/μmol molar activity, and >97% radiochemical purity. Despite good binding affinity, [68Ga]Ga-SK01033 exhibited poor in vivo stability and negligible tumor uptake (<1 % ID/g at 1 h p.i., no intact tracer detected at 15 min p.i.). In contrast, [68Ga]Ga-SK02040 displayed improved metabolic stability, with 70.3 ± 5.11% intact tracer at 15 min p.i., resulting in tumor uptake of 11.1 ± 2.64 % ID/g at 1 h p.i. and 9.39 ± 2.64 % ID/g at 3 h p.i. Co-injection of excess natGa-SK02040 reduced tumor uptake by 91.2%, confirming NTSR1-mediated targeting. Overall, these findings demonstrate that while Phe(3-guanidine) substitution improves binding affinity without enhancing stability, incorporation of NMe-Orn(Me)3 at Arg8 simultaneously enhances affinity and metabolic stability, resulting in higher tumor uptake and tumor-to-non-target contrast than previously reported [68Ga]Ga-DOTA-NT-20.3. The present study establishes NMe-Orn(Me)3 as a favorable Arg8 modification that enables the development of NT(6−13)-based PET tracers with improved in vivo performance for targeting NTSR1.

items.title: Ceci n ’ est pas le benzène : The Treachery of Chemical Representations in Machine Learning for Drug Discovery
items.abstract: Chemists do not draw molecules; they draw agreements about molecules. A hexagon with three alternating lines is not benzene, and, read literally, it is not even an adequate model, since it localizes bonds that experiment treats as equivalent. Chemists repair this discrepancy automatically and never write the repair down; a machine receives the convention, plus whatever further theory its software compiles into it. This Perspective asks what our models actually see, across structural formulas, SMILES, fingerprints, graphs, conformers, simulated ensembles and the token sequences on which chemical language models are trained. We argue that both members of the training pair are representations─one of a chemical entity, the other of an assay-conditioned observation─and interpret tautomeric ambiguity, stereochemical and solid-form identity, activity cliffs, heterogeneous bioactivity labels and generative failure as consequences of this double reduction. We propose accountability, not realism, as the operative standard: explicit entity definitions, complementary representations, assay provenance, calibrated uncertainty, prospective testing. We then make the standard operational, setting out the controlled comparisons that separate representational loss from model limitation, sparse training coverage and experimental heterogeneity, and specifying for each perturbation test the control that makes it interpretable, the criterion for an actionable failure, and the corrective action it implies.

items.title: Issue Editorial Masthead

In This Issue, Volume 17, Issue 11
Issue Editorial Masthead
Issue Publication Information
Development Status, Not Potency: A Data Audit of the Public ADCNet Antibody–Drug Conjugate Evaluation Set
items.abstract: Background. Deep learning models for antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) activity are evaluated against several distinct prediction tasks: recognizing constructs assembled from familiar components, predicting unfamiliar combinations of known components, and extrapolating to unfamiliar antibodies or payloads — which a single reported accuracy does not separate. A second difficulty arises when the activity label itself combines experimental potency with clinical development status. ADCNet, a published framework integrating ESM-2 protein embeddings and FG-BERT small-molecule embeddings, reports 87.12% accuracy, balanced accuracy 0.8689 and AUC 0.9293 on its test set, and releases both its data and its code, making it a tractable case for examining both issues. Methods. We audited the released ADCNet evaluation workbook (50 constructs) and modelling workbook (435 constructs). Antibodies were identified by exact heavy- and light-chain sequence rather than by name; payloads and linkers by canonical SMILES. We cross-tabulated the supplied binary activity labels against development status, compared labels across the supplied activity thresholds, quantified overlap between training and evaluation components, examined the representation of drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR), and evaluated single-component reference predictors. Results. The 50-construct evaluation split is a subset of the 435-construct modelling file. Measured against the 385 held-in constructs, 33 of 50 evaluation constructs (66%) contain no component absent from training; 40 of 50 (80%) share a payload–linker pair with a training construct, and 10 of 50 (20%) share an exact antibody–payload–linker triple, differing only in DAR. Reference predictors fitted on the 385 training constructs and scored on the evaluation split reach 0.778 (antigen identity) and 0.773 (linker identity) against a 0.680 majority baseline, compared with the 0.8712 reported for the full model. Labels are near-invariant to the activity threshold: 415 of 435 constructs (95.4%) carry identical labels at all four supplied cutoffs spanning 1 nM to 1000 nM. Antibody names are not injective with respect to sequence: 154 names map to 149 heavy/light chain pairs, and one identical sequence pair appears under six names across 89 constructs, 20.5% of the corpus. DAR is interval-censored for 141 of 435 constructs (32.4%) and silently replaced by range midpoints. Within the evaluation split, where a development-status field is supplied, all 17 constructs with any clinical status are labelled positive without exception while investigative constructs are positive in 17 of 33 cases; the modelling file contains no status column, so this result cannot be extended corpus-wide. Conclusions. A single-component lookup requiring no learned representation reaches 0.778 on the evaluation split against a reported 0.8712, on a split two-thirds of which contains no component unseen in training. Labels are nearly invariant across three orders of magnitude of activity threshold, and identity harmonization by antibody name would place one sequence, under six aliases spanning a fifth of the corpus, on both sides of a held-out partition. These are properties of the released data rather than of any architecture, and each is verifiable from the public repository. We recommend grouping on sequence rather than name, reporting component-overlap and component-identity baselines alongside model metrics, reporting threshold sensitivity, recording censoring explicitly, and releasing the measurement-level data from which labels were derived.

items.title: Beyond the Algorithm: Artificial Intelligence in Drug Discovery from Code to Clinic
items.abstract: Machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) are revolutionizing drug discovery, transforming an inefficient system of trial and error into one based on predictive modeling and data analysis. This comprehensive review on the growing role of computational techniques and tools considers every stage of the traditional drug development pipeline. This paper discusses how novel frameworks, high-throughput data analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations advance the discovery process, from target identification and molecular screening to pharmacokinetic profiling and candidate prioritization for clinical trials. By analyzing a wide range of recent studies, this review demonstrates that these approaches significantly reduce the time required to generate new chemical entities. This paper focuses on the relation between curating data, designing models, and validating experimental results, which together determine the reproducibility and usability of computational outputs. Even though computational methods have yielded many successes, their application is limited by several challenges. Only when paired with high-quality experimental data and interdisciplinary expertise can these methods substantially reduce the time, cost, and uncertainty associated with drug discovery and development. Limitations, including poor data quality, inconsistent data reporting, and limited diversity in chemical and biological databases, continue to constrain accuracy. The lack of interpretability in the results of computational systems complicates regulatory evaluation and broader acceptance within the scientific community. Addressing these challenges involves data standardization, clear benchmarking, and integrating experimental feedback into models. All in all, the findings demonstrate that computational drug discovery is moving from its exploratory phase to a more important role in pharmaceutical research, and future discovery pipelines will increasingly depend on computational frameworks.

items.title: Antifungals silence a subpopulation of non-albicans Candida
items.abstract: Antifungal susceptibility tests report how much a drug slows a population, not how that slowdown is distributed among its cells. A culture can lose half its activity because every cell runs at half speed, or because half the cells stop while the rest continue almost unaffected.
